lec.t0.0.dit: Hi! Let's explore the Terminaworld together. Where is the “you are here” sign?
lec.t0.0.bravo: Found it, there's our “you are here” sign! Grown-ups call it “the folder you're in” (`pwd`).
lec.t0.0.adulte: `pwd` (print working directory) prints the absolute path of the current folder, from the root /. Same in a real Linux or macOS terminal.
lec.t0.1.dit: Look around you: what is there in this place?
lec.t0.1.bravo: Everything in this place! Grown-ups say “list the folder”.
lec.t0.1.adulte: `ls` (list) shows the contents of the current folder: files and subfolders, without the hidden ones (those starting with a dot).
lec.t0.2.dit: Come on, let's go back to base camp!
lec.t0.2.bravo: Back at base camp! Grown-ups say “your home folder”; its nickname is ~.
lec.t0.2.adulte: `~` means your home directory ($HOME); `cd ~` (or just `cd`) goes back there from anywhere.
lec.t1.0.dit: I need an adventure zone to play in, inside the Terminaworld. From your base camp, build a new place!
lec.t1.0.bravo: A brand-new place! Grown-ups say “create a folder”.
lec.t1.0.adulte: `mkdir` (make directory) creates a folder in the current folder. The game only builds inside this folder, ~/terrain_terminagotchi.
lec.t1.1.bravo: Here we are! Walking to a place, grown-ups say “change folder”.
lec.t1.1.adulte: `cd name` enters a subfolder: it's a relative path, it leaves from the current folder.
lec.t1.2.dit: Build me a little nest here!
lec.t1.2.bravo: It's perfect! A place inside a place: grown-ups say “a subfolder”. And I can hear a noise far away…
lec.t1.2.adulte: `mkdir nid` creates a subfolder; `mkdir -p a/b/c` would also create the folders in between.
lec.t2.0.dit: I'm hungry! Take the funnel “>” and pour an apple onto the scroll repas.txt in my nest.
lec.t2.0.bravo: Yum! Careful: the funnel wipes the scroll before writing. Grown-ups say “write to a file”.
lec.t2.0.adulte: `echo` writes its text to standard output; `>` redirects it into a file (created, or overwritten if it exists).
lec.t2.1.dit: Read me the scroll repas.txt out loud.
lec.t2.1.bravo: An apple, perfect! Grown-ups say “display a file”. Always check before you act!
lec.t2.1.adulte: `cat` (concatenate) prints the contents of a file; nid/repas.txt is a relative path.
lec.t2.2.dit: Take the detective's magnifying glass: look for the word “pomme” on the scroll.
lec.t2.2.bravo: The magnifying glass found it! Grown-ups say “search in a file”.
lec.t2.2.adulte: `grep pattern file` prints the lines that contain the pattern (a regular expression); `-i` ignores case.
lec.t3.0.dit: Who is allowed to touch my meal? Look at the padlocks.
lec.t3.0.bravo: r = read, w = write, x = make it run. Grown-ups say “permissions”.
lec.t3.0.adulte: `ls -l` (long format) shows the permissions (r read, w write, x execute) for the owner, the group and others, then owner, size and date.
lec.t3.0.bravo.win: R = read-only (no padlock yet). Grown-ups say “attributes”.
lec.t3.1.dit: Put a padlock on the scroll so nobody damages it!
lec.t3.1.bravo: Click! You can read it, but not write anymore. Grown-ups say “read-only”.
lec.t3.1.adulte: `chmod 444` sets the permissions r--r--r--: everyone can read, nobody can write until the w right is given back (the owner can do it with `chmod u+w`; root writes anyway). 4 = r, 2 = w, 1 = x.
lec.t3.2.dit: Try adding a pear at the bottom of the scroll, just to see…
lec.t3.2.bravo: Refused! “>>” adds at the bottom without wiping anything… but the padlock holds. Grown-ups say “append”.
lec.t3.2.adulte: `>>` appends to the end of the file; here writing fails ("Permission denied") because the file no longer has the w permission.
lec.t4.0.dit: Make a photocopy of my meal, just in case.
lec.t4.0.bravo: Two identical scrolls, and the original didn't move! Grown-ups say “copy”.
lec.t4.0.adulte: `cp source destination` copies a file; the original stays. `cp -r` copies a whole folder.
lec.t4.1.dit: Carry the copy to the crossroads and stick a new label on it: reserve.txt.
lec.t4.1.bravo: Carried and renamed in one go! Grown-ups say “move” and “rename”.
lec.t4.1.adulte: `mv` moves and renames at the same time: reserve.txt is the new name, in the current folder.
lec.t4.2.dit: We don't need it anymore. Careful: this is the shredder, not the bin!
lec.t4.2.astuce: If it asks for confirmation, answer y.
lec.t4.2.bravo: Shredded forever: no bin to get it back. Grown-ups say “delete”. Always check first!
lec.t4.2.adulte: `rm` deletes for good, with no recycle bin. Pros check with `ls` first (or use `rm -i`).
lec.reseau.desc: talking with the other worlds (the internet)
lec.reseau0.0.dit: Is anyone in the world next door? Shout “Ahoy!” (a `ping`) and listen for the echo.
lec.reseau0.0.bravo: Each echo is a round trip; the time it takes (in ms) is the latency.
lec.reseau0.0.adulte: `ping -c 3` sends 3 ICMP "echo" packets and measures the reply time (-c: number of packets; without -c, it goes on until Ctrl+C).
lec.reseau0.1.dit: And what is our world's address (our IP address)?
lec.reseau0.1.bravo: Here's our IP address: our world's number on the network.
lec.reseau0.1.adulte: `ip a` (or `ifconfig`) lists the network interfaces and their IP addresses (127.0.0.1 = the machine itself).
lec.reseau1.0.dit: Send `curl`, the mail carrier, to knock at a website's entrance without going in.
lec.reseau1.0.bravo: HTTP answer code: 200 = “come in!”, 404 = not found, 500 = the site is sick.
lec.reseau1.0.adulte: `curl -I` sends an HTTP HEAD request: it prints only the response headers (code 200, type, size).
lec.reseau1.1.dit: From the playground folder, download a web page into colis.html.
lec.reseau1.1.bravo: -o = “output”: the answer is stored in a file, like the postman dropping off a letter.
lec.reseau1.1.adulte: `curl -o file URL` downloads the resource into a file (-o: output). Without a network, the game drops a backup page.
lec.reseau1.2.dit: Show the first 5 lines of the parcel.
lec.reseau1.2.bravo: HTML: the language web pages are written in!
lec.reseau1.2.adulte: `head -n 5` prints the first 5 lines: here the start of the page's HTML code.
lec.reseau2.0.dit: Ask the DNS (the directory of worlds): which IP address for example.com?
lec.reseau2.0.bravo: The DNS turns names (example.com) into IP addresses.
lec.reseau2.0.adulte: `nslookup` queries DNS: it translates a domain name into an IP address.
lec.reseau2.1.dit: Follow our packets' journey, from router to router, all the way to the site.
lec.reseau2.1.bravo: Each line = one router crossed. The internet is a chain of relays!
lec.reseau2.1.adulte: `traceroute` shows each router crossed on the way to the destination, with the time of each hop.
lec.git.desc: the camera for your files (`git` needed)
lec.git0.0.dit: From the crossroads of the Terminaworld, make a magic photo album for your objects: the notebook.
lec.git0.0.bravo: The album is ready! It keeps its photos in a secret passage, .git. Grown-ups say “a `git` repository”.
lec.git0.0.adulte: `git init carnet` creates the carnet folder and an empty Git repository (the hidden .git folder) that will keep the history.
lec.git0.1.adulte: `cd carnet`: git commands act on the repository of the current folder.
lec.git0.2.dit: Ask the camera what it sees.
lec.git0.2.bravo: It tells you what changed. `git status`: pros type it 100 times a day.
lec.git0.2.adulte: `git status` shows the state of the repository: files that are modified, added to the index, or unknown to Git.
lec.git1.0.dit: Write the first page of the diary in a new file.
lec.git1.0.bravo: `git` saw a new file… but hasn't taken the photo yet: it is “untracked”.
lec.git1.0.adulte: `echo "jour 1" > journal.txt` creates the file with one line of text.
lec.git1.1.dit: Add the file to the index (put it in front of the lens).
lec.git1.1.bravo: `git add` puts the file in the index: it will be in the next photo.
lec.git1.1.adulte: `git add` puts the file in the index (staging area): the list of what will go into the next commit.
lec.git1.2.dit: Make your first commit (click, the photo)!
lec.git1.2.astuce: If `git` asks your name: `git config --global user.name "Your name"` (same for user.email)
lec.git1.2.bravo: A commit = a photo of your files at this moment, with a message. Forever.
lec.git1.2.adulte: `git commit -m` records a snapshot of the index with a message; Git needs a name and an e-mail (git config).
lec.git2.0.dit: Add a line at the end of the diary (>>).
lec.git2.0.bravo: The file has changed since the last commit…
lec.git2.0.adulte: `>>` appends a line to the end of the file without erasing the rest.
lec.git2.1.dit: Show the diff: what changed since the commit.
lec.git2.1.bravo: + in green = line added, - in red = line removed.
lec.git2.1.adulte: `git diff` shows the differences between the files and the last commit (+ added, - removed).
lec.git2.2.dit: Show the history of commits (the album).
lec.git2.2.astuce: Type q to leave the display.
lec.git2.2.bravo: Each commit has a unique ID (its hash).
lec.git2.2.adulte: `git log` lists the commits from newest to oldest, with author, date and message (q to quit).
lec.scripts.desc: recipes the world follows on its own, and YOUR commands
lec.scripts0.0.dit: From the crossroads, write a recipe (a list of commands) in my nest.
lec.scripts0.0.bravo: A recipe stored in a file: grown-ups say “a script”.
lec.scripts0.0.adulte: a script is a text file that contains commands; `echo '…' > nid/miam.sh` writes it in one line.
lec.scripts0.1.dit: Ask the world to follow the recipe!
lec.scripts0.1.bravo: The world followed the script all by itself. You just programmed!
lec.scripts0.1.adulte: `sh file` starts a new shell that runs the file's commands, line by line.
lec.scripts1.0.dit: Allow the recipe to cook on its own: make it executable (able to do something).
lec.scripts1.0.bravo: x = executable: the script has become a program.
lec.scripts1.0.adulte: `chmod +x` adds the execute permission: the script can then run directly (./miam.sh, with a first line #!/bin/sh).
lec.scripts1.1.dit: Give the recipe a nickname: create the alias “miam”.
lec.scripts1.1.bravo: An alias is a nickname for a command. You created a command that didn't exist!
lec.scripts1.1.adulte: `alias name='command'` creates a shortcut, valid only in this terminal while it stays open.
lec.scripts1.2.bravo: YUM! It's the best command in the world.
lec.scripts1.2.adulte: the shell replaces the alias with its text before running it; a function, on the other hand, is called like a small command.
lec.scripts2.0.dit: Your alias will vanish when the terminal closes. Write it in your configuration file (the camp's notebook)!
lec.scripts2.0.adulte: `>> ~/.bashrc` adds the alias to the file read each time a bash terminal opens (~/.zshrc for zsh): it becomes permanent.
lec.scripts2.1.bravo: From now on, your own inventions feed me ×3!
lec.scripts2.1.adulte: `source ~/.bashrc` re-reads the file in the current shell, without closing the terminal.
lec.systeme.desc: watching over the world and its inhabitants (the system)
lec.systeme0.0.dit: Who is the boss of this world (the user)?
lec.systeme0.0.adulte: `whoami` prints the current user's name; `id` also gives their number (UID) and groups.
lec.systeme0.1.dit: Who is awake in the world? List the processes.
lec.systeme0.1.bravo: Each line is a process (an awake program), with its number: the PID.
lec.systeme0.1.adulte: `ps` lists the processes with their number (PID); `ps aux` shows those of all users (on a phone, an app only sees its own).
lec.systeme1.0.dit: Is there any room left in the big chest (the disk)?
lec.systeme1.0.adulte: `df -h` (disk free) shows the used and free space of each mounted filesystem.
lec.systeme1.1.dit: How heavy is the playground folder?
lec.systeme1.1.bravo: du = “disk usage”. Handy to find what fills up the disk.
lec.systeme1.1.adulte: `du -sh` prints the total size of a folder, in readable units.
lec.systeme2.0.dit: Start a process in the background (it takes a nap at the far end of the world).
lec.systeme2.0.bravo: & = “in the background”: the terminal stays free.
lec.systeme2.0.adulte: `&` runs the command in the background: the terminal gives the prompt back at once; `sleep 300` waits 300 seconds.
lec.systeme2.1.dit: Find it in the list of jobs.
lec.systeme2.1.bravo: There it is, with its job number.
lec.systeme2.1.adulte: `jobs` lists the jobs started from this terminal, with their number (%1, %2…).
lec.systeme2.2.bravo: Process stopped. Handy when a program is stuck!
lec.systeme2.2.adulte: `kill %1` sends the SIGTERM signal to job number 1; `kill PID` does the same with a process number.
lec.android.desc: drive your phone: apps, links, tools
lec.android0.0.dit: Make a little note pop up on the phone's screen.
lec.android0.0.astuce: You need the Termux:API app and: pkg install termux-api
lec.android0.0.bravo: Termux:API is the bridge between the terminal and the phone.
lec.android0.0.adulte: `termux-toast` (termux-api package) shows a short notification on the screen.
lec.android0.2.adulte: `termux-torch on` turns on the camera flash (camera permission required).
lec.android0.3.bravo: You control the phone's hardware in one line.
lec.android0.3.adulte: `off` turns the torch off; in the app, `lampe` uses Android's CameraManager API, like termux-torch in Termux.
lec.android1.0.dit: Open the window onto a website, in your browser.
lec.android1.0.bravo: Android picks the right app for this link all by itself.
lec.android1.0.adulte: `termux-open-url` asks Android to open the address in the default browser.
lec.android1.1.dit: Unfold the map to find a place.
lec.android1.1.bravo: An “intent” = a request sent to Android: “show me this”.
lec.android1.1.adulte: a VIEW "intent" with a geo: address opens the maps app; in Termux: `am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d geo:…`.
lec.android1.2.bravo: DIAL opens the keypad with the number: you decide whether to call.
lec.android1.2.adulte: `am start` with the DIAL action opens the phone's dialler with the number, without calling.
lec.android2.0.dit: Every app has a secret name: its package. Find the one for Settings.
lec.android2.0.adulte: `pm list packages` lists the identifiers of the installed apps; `grep` keeps those that contain the word.
lec.android2.1.astuce: If nothing opens: allow Termux to “display over other apps”.
lec.android2.1.bravo: MAIN + LAUNCHER = “open it as if you tapped its icon”.
lec.android2.1.adulte: `am start` (activity manager) launches an app's main activity (MAIN/LAUNCHER) from its package.
lec.android2.2.dit: That's long to type… write your function “`ouvre`” in ~/.bashrc, forever!
lec.android2.2.adulte: a shell function `name() { … }` written in ~/.bashrc is reloaded every time the terminal opens; "$1" is its first argument.
lec.android2.3.adulte: `source ~/.bashrc` re-reads the configuration in the current shell.
lec.android2.4.bravo: You switch your apps on from the keyboard, like a pro.
lec.android2.4.adulte: the function is called like a command; its argument replaces $1.
lec.android3.0.dit: How much food is left in the phone's tummy (the battery)?
lec.android3.0.bravo: percentage = the percentage, status = charging or not.
lec.android3.0.adulte: `termux-battery-status` prints the battery state as JSON (percentage, charging, temperature).
lec.android3.1.adulte: `termux-tts-speak` reads the text with Android's speech synthesis.
lec.android3.2.dit: Put some text in the phone's magic pocket: the clipboard.
lec.android3.2.bravo: Paste it wherever you like: it's in the clipboard.
lec.android3.2.adulte: `termux-clipboard-set` copies the text to Android's clipboard.

aide.rencontre.examiner: `cat` reads {un_fichier} out loud. The monster's card is placed in {terrain}.
aide.rencontre.repaire: `find` looks for an object in every place, even the tiniest (each {dossier} and its subfolders). It gives you the full path: that's where the monster lives.
aide.fichiers.enclos: `mkdir` builds a new place (“make directory”: create a folder).
aide.fichiers.gamelle: `touch` puts down a brand-new object (an empty file). The / separates the place from the object.
aide.fichiers.doudou: `cp` makes a magic photocopy: first the object to copy, then the place to put it. The original doesn't move.
aide.fichiers.renomme: `mv` carries an object somewhere else; if it stays in the same place, it just changes its label (its name).
aide.fichiers.archive: `tar` packs a whole place into one tightly packed suitcase (an archive): c = create, z = squash (compress), f = name of the suitcase.
aide.reseau.ping: `ping` shouts “Ahoy!” at another world and waits for the echo. localhost = your own world. -c 3 = shout 3 times, then stop.
aide.reseau.hote: `hostname` tells the name of your world on the network.
aide.reseau.ip: Every world connected to the network has an address, like a postal address: {ip}. `ip a` shows them all.
aide.reseau.dns: `nslookup` opens {dns}: it turns a website's name into an address.
aide.reseau.page: `curl` is a postman: it fetches a page from a website. -o picks the box to store it in.
aide.processus.ps: `ps` shows who is awake: every {processus}. `ps aux` shows them all, even the other inhabitants' ones.
aide.processus.fond: sleep 120 waits 120 seconds. The & sends it to nap at the far end of the world (in the background): you keep control.
aide.processus.jobs: jobs shows the programs you sent to the back, with their number.
aide.processus.kill: `kill` sends a program to bed (it stops it). %1 = program number 1 in the jobs list.
aide.memoire.place: `df` shows the free room in {disque}; -h writes sizes for humans (GB, MB).
aide.memoire.ram: free shows {ram}: a big worktop where programs put their things. -h = readable sizes.
aide.memoire.poids: du weighs a place and everything in it; -s = just the total, -h = readable size.
aide.memoire.sac: `ls sac` looks into the bag. The | is a pipe: it pours the list into `wc -l`, which counts the lines. Then say the number with `echo`.
aide.securite.cage: `touch` puts down a brand-new object (build the pen first with `mkdir` if it's missing).
aide.securite.cachette: An object whose name starts with a dot is hidden: `ls` doesn't see it, `ls -a` does.
aide.securite.prive: `chmod` puts on a padlock (it changes the permissions). 600 = only you can read and write, nobody else.
aide.securite.empreinte: `sha256sum` takes the fingerprint of an object: a string of letters and numbers that changes if you change a single letter. Copy the first 8 with `echo`.
aide.code.chant: `echo` says a text. The funnel > writes it on a scroll instead of the screen.
aide.code.script: A recipe (a script) is a scroll of commands. Write it, then `chmod +x` allows it to cook by itself: it becomes {executable} (you run it with `./tour.sh`).
aide.code.compte: A for loop repeats a command for each number. Everything said lands on the scroll thanks to the funnel >.
aide.materiel.machine: `uname -m` tells what kind of brain the world has: {processeur} (x86_64, arm64…).
aide.materiel.coeurs: `nproc` counts the cores of {processeur}: how many things it does at the same time. Then answer with `echo`.
aide.materiel.disques: lsblk shows {disque} and its compartments (the partitions).
aide.bugs.erreurs: `grep` is the detective's magnifying glass: it shows the lines that contain the word.
aide.bugs.combien: `grep -c` counts the lines found by the magnifying glass, instead of showing them.
aide.bugs.corrige: `grep -v` does the opposite and keeps the lines WITHOUT the word; the funnel > writes them on a new scroll.
aide.nuage.photos: `touch` can put down several objects at once: write their names one after another.
aide.nuage.copie: `cp -r` photocopies a whole place, with everything in it (r = recursive).
aide.donnees.debut: `head` reads only the top of the scroll (10 lines).
aide.donnees.lignes: `wc -l` counts the lines of a scroll. Then answer with `echo`.
aide.donnees.trie: sort puts the lines in order like a dictionary; the funnel > writes the result on a scroll.
aide.donnees.differentes: sort sorts, `uniq` removes twins that follow each other, `wc -l` counts. The pipes | connect them one after another.
aide.crypto.decode: base64 disguises a text as strange letters (it encodes it). `base64 -d` takes the disguise off (d = decode).
aide.crypto.empreinte: `sha256sum` takes the unique fingerprint of an object. Copy the first 8 characters with `echo`.
aide.ia.bonjour: `echo` says the text you give it.
aide.ia.chat: `grep -c` counts the lines where the magnifying glass finds the word.
aide.ia.frequent: sort sorts, `uniq -c` counts each word, then `sort -n` sorts by number: the last one is the champion.
aide.retro.record: `sort -n` puts numbers from smallest to biggest; `tail -1` keeps the last one (the biggest).
aide.retro.top3: `sort -nr` sorts from biggest to smallest (r = reversed), `head -3` keeps the first 3, the funnel > writes them on the scroll.
aide.glitch.repare: `rev` flips each line, like in a mirror; the funnel > writes the result on a scroll.
aide.glitch.chuchote: tr changes letters into other letters: here each capital (A-Z) into lowercase (a-z). The < hands it the scroll to read.
aide.systeme.qui: `whoami` (“who am I?”) tells your resident name: your username.
aide.systeme.systeme: `uname -a` reads the world's ID card: its name, its version, its kind of brain.
aide.systeme.alias: An alias is a nickname: a short word that runs a longer command. Then type the nickname to try it!
aide.systeme.variable: An environment variable is a little box with a label that the whole terminal can open. export fills it; `echo $BESTIOLE` reads it back.

lec.terrain.refait.dit: I put {fichiers} back in place so the lesson can go on.
lec.terrain.recule.dit: An object from the lesson has disappeared: let's redo the previous step.
app.terrain.titre: 🏚 The adventure zone has disappeared: rebuild it
app.terrain.pourquoi: Without a playroom, no lessons and no monsters. If you can't do it, I'll rebuild it myself in a few commands.
dress.combat.debut: ⚔ Battle! {nom} faces {monstre}. Type `{cmd}` for its special attack, `ls` to observe, or any command to attack.
dress.combat.coups: Every command you type is a move:
dress.combat.observer.aide: observe: you dodge, and your next move is sure to hit
dress.combat.observe: {nom} watches {monstre}: ATK {atk}, DEF {def}. Next hit guaranteed!
dress.combat.gagne: Victory! {monstre} is less afraid of you: taming it will be easier.
dress.combat.perdu: {nom} is KO… Nothing serious: a little 5-minute nap. The taming starts anyway!
dress.combat.nul: End of the battle: nobody won. The taming begins!
dress.combat.tous_repos: Your troop is resting: no battle this time.
dress.combat.ensuite: After the battle (5 turns at most): the taming.

hist.reveil.debut: Here I am, out of the egg! This world, the Terminaworld, has been asleep for so long… Grown-ups call it “the computer”. Come: we'll explore it together, and I'll show you where I was hiding!
hist.reveil.fin: *CRACK!* You found me! I'm not alone in the dark anymore. But the world is still asleep, and I can hear monsters snoring far away… First I need a nest of my own.
hist.nid.debut: Brrr, the old hallway is so draughty! Let's build ourselves a nest: {un_dossier} just for us, with a bed and a meal. Commands are our tools, like a hammer and nails.
hist.nid.fin: My nest is perfect and my tummy is full! Listen carefully: seven places of the world are asleep, and in each one a family of monsters has settled. The ancients gave them funny names, written on the signposts. You choose where to start.
hist.grenier.debut: Here's the Attic, a forest where the Sylvans pile up everything they find! Their vines have mixed everything up, and my teddy bear is stuck somewhere. We need the map of the forest, then to tidy, copy and throw away what's no longer needed.
hist.grenier.fin: The forest can breathe! The vines have tidied themselves away and the Sylvans are napping in the branches. You can carry, copy and throw away like a real adventurer.
hist.cave.debut: Shh… can you hear that? Deep in the Cellar, a cavern dug under the mountain, the Demons steal my food at night! To stop them, we need to know who's in charge in this world, then put {droits} on my supplies.
hist.cave.fin: Click, clack, padlock! The Demons tried and broke their teeth. They promised to be good… well, almost.
hist.bibliotheque.debut: At the bottom of the lagoon sleeps a sunken library… and the Book of the Abyss has disappeared! The Abyssals hid it between the seaweed-covered shelves, and without it, we can't read the story of the world. Grab your magnifying glass: let's investigate.
hist.bibliotheque.fin: Book found! The Abyssals even taught us to count lines and search for words. You are a real detective of {fichiers}.
hist.machines.debut: The world is suffocating! At the foot of the volcano, the Elementals have blocked the pipes of the old engine room. Let's look at the room left in {ram} and in {disque}, find what's too heavy… and throw it away.
hist.machines.fin: Vrrrooom! The machines are running again and the Elementals are warming up by the lava. The world is breathing deeply.
hist.dortoir.debut: Woo woo… In the Dormitory, a valley full of mist, ghost {processus} refuse to sleep! The Undead keep waking them up. We'll count them, start one ourselves, then send them to bed.
hist.dortoir.fin: Silence… everyone is asleep under the mist. The Undead yawn and wave at us. You know who is awake in the world, and how to put them to bed.
hist.atelier.debut: In the middle of the scrap-metal hills, in the Workshop, the Constructs build machines that follow recipes all by themselves! We'll write {script}, make it work, give it a nickname… and take photos of our objects with the magic camera, `git`.
hist.atelier.fin: Bzzt! The Constructs clap their pincers. You wrote your own commands and took your first photos of objects. You're a real inventor!
hist.tour.debut: At the very top of the Tower, among clouds and lightning, the Celestials watch {reseau}. Our world is not alone! We'll shout “Ahoy!” to the other worlds, find our address, send the mail carrier and read the directory.
hist.tour.fin: Ahoy, ahoy! The other worlds answered! The Celestials show us the secret tunnel, `ssh`, which we'll open one day. Our world is not alone anymore.
hist.coeur.debut: The heart of the world is beating very softly… The Aberrations scrambled everything: the messages are backwards and the heart is in pieces. You'll need everything you've learned. And deep down, someone enormous is sleeping: Abyssor.
hist.coeur.fin: Boom… boom… BOOM! The heart is beating! Everyone wakes up, the sun rises over every place, and Abyssor opens one eye: “Thank you, little human.” He goes back to sleep with a smile. You woke up the Terminaworld!
hist.telephone.debut: At the edge of the world, there's a garden: your phone! You can turn on its torch, make it vibrate, open apps… Let's go play outside.
hist.telephone.fin: The phone garden has no secrets for you now. You control it from the keyboard, like a pro!
hist.entree.dit: Let's go! Walk to the place {piece}.
hist.entree.adulte: a path that starts with `~/` is absolute: the shell replaces ~ with your home folder, so the command works from anywhere.
hist.reveil1.0.dit: Look around your base camp: an old path is called terrain_terminagotchi. Follow it!
hist.reveil1.0.bravo: Crrrr… So much dust! Here we are at the crossroads of the sleeping Terminaworld.
hist.reveil1.0.adulte: `cd terrain_terminagotchi` enters the game's folder, under your home folder: it's a relative path.
hist.reveil1.1.dit: It's pitch dark. Look around you: what's here?
hist.reveil1.1.bravo: A signpost: the vestibule, the old entrance of the world. It looks like something warm is waiting for me there…
hist.reveil1.1.adulte: `ls` lists the current folder: here, a single folder, `vestibule`. An empty folder would print nothing (no message = no error).
hist.reveil1.2.bravo: We're in the vestibule, under the old stone arch. Shh…
hist.reveil1.2.adulte: `cd vestibule`: a relative path to a subfolder of the current folder.
hist.reveil1.3.bravo: My old shell! This is where you found me, safe inside my egg. Thank you!
hist.reveil1.3.adulte: `ls` shows the objects in the hall: among them, oeuf_tout_chaud.txt, the file the game left there. A file is an object of the world.
hist.nid0.0.dit: I need a nest. Go up one step, to the crossroads: `cd ..` means “go to the place that contains this one” (the parent place).
hist.nid0.0.adulte: `..` means the parent folder: `cd ..` goes up one level in the tree.
hist.nid0.2.dit: Put a brand-new object in the nest: it will be my bed.
hist.nid0.2.bravo: A brand-new bed, empty and soft. Grown-ups say “create {un_fichier} that's empty”.
hist.nid0.2.adulte: `touch` creates an empty file (or updates its date if it exists); nid/lit.txt is a relative path.
hist.grenier0.1.dit: Vines everywhere! Look at the map of the whole forest at once.
hist.grenier0.1.bravo: So many places inside places! That's {arborescence}.
hist.grenier0.1.adulte: `tree` shows the directory tree (if installed); `ls -R` gives the same contents, folder by folder.
hist.grenier0.2.dit: My teddy bear is stuck in the mess! Bring it back to the nest.
hist.grenier0.2.bravo: My teddy! `mv` carried it all the way to the nest. “..” means “the parent place”, the one that contains the attic: the crossroads.
hist.grenier0.2.adulte: `mv source destination/` moves the file; ../nid/ goes up one level then into nid.
hist.t4.3.dit: Expert challenge: photocopy the whole jumble at once, with all its places.
hist.t4.3.bravo: -r means "with everything inside" (recursive). Well done, expert!
hist.t4.3.adulte: `cp -r` (recursive) copies a folder with all its subfolders and files.
hist.cave0.2.dit: The keeper's key is called `sudo`: it's for big jobs, not for playing. Just read its instructions.
hist.cave0.2.astuce: -h asks for no password. Never give your password to a game!
hist.cave0.2.bravo: `sudo` means "do it as {administrateur}". With it you can fix everything… or break everything. That's why it asks for a password.
hist.cave0.2.adulte: `sudo` runs a command as root (the administrator) after your password. `sudo -h` only shows the help, without running anything.
hist.biblio0.1.dit: The Book of the Abyss is hidden on a shelf. Ask `find` to look for it everywhere.
hist.biblio0.1.bravo: Found it! `find` searches every place and every place inside places.
hist.biblio0.1.adulte: `find . -name "*abysses*"` walks the current folder (.) and its subfolders; * is a wildcard, the quotes stop the shell from expanding it too early.
hist.biblio0.2.dit: Open the book and read it.
hist.biblio0.2.bravo: What a story! `less` turns the pages one by one.
hist.biblio0.2.adulte: `less` shows a file page by page (space: next page, /word: search, q: quit). On the phone, `cat` shows it all at once.
hist.biblio1.1.dit: Read only the beginning of the book: its first 3 lines.
hist.biblio1.1.bravo: `head` reads the top of the page, like a newspaper headline.
hist.biblio1.1.adulte: `head -n 3` prints the first 3 lines (10 by default); `tail` does the same with the end.
hist.biblio1.2.dit: How many lines does this book have? Count them!
hist.biblio1.2.bravo: `wc` counts lines (-l), words (-w) and letters. Handy for a detective!
hist.biblio1.2.adulte: `wc -l` (word count, lines) counts the lines of a file; `-w` counts the words.
hist.biblio1.3.dit: Expert challenge: the word TRESOR is written somewhere in the sunken library. Search all the books at once.
hist.biblio1.3.bravo: -r searches every shelf, -n gives the line number. Bravo, expert!
hist.biblio1.3.adulte: `grep -rn` searches recursively (-r) in all files and prints the line number (-n).
hist.machines0.1.dit: Listen to the world breathing: how much room is left in {ram}?
hist.machines0.1.bravo: free shows {ram}: the world's worktable. When it's full, everything slows down!
hist.machines0.1.adulte: `free -h` shows the used and free memory (RAM), in readable units (-h: human-readable).
hist.machines0.2.dit: Something heavy is blocking the pipes. Weigh everything in this place.
hist.machines0.2.bravo: vieux_carton.bin is heavy! That's the culprit.
hist.machines0.2.adulte: `du -sh *` (disk usage) prints the total size (-s) of each item, in readable units (-h); * means everything here.
hist.machines0.3.dit: Throw away that old box (only that one, and only here!).
hist.machines0.3.bravo: Phew! The world breathes better. There's room again in {disque}.
hist.machines0.3.adulte: `rm file` deletes just this one file. The game created it on purpose in the adventure zone.
hist.atelier0.1.dit: The Constructs left a plan on the workbench. Read it!
hist.atelier0.1.bravo: A three-step plan: write a recipe, make it work, and take a photo of everything. Let's get to work!
hist.atelier0.1.adulte: `cat` prints the whole text file: ideal for a short plan.
hist.tour2.1.dit: To get into another world, there's a secret tunnel: `ssh`. We won't open it today, just ask it who it is.
hist.tour2.1.bravo: `ssh` links two worlds with an encrypted tunnel. You need the other world's key to get in.
hist.tour2.1.adulte: `ssh` (Secure Shell) opens an encrypted session on another machine; `ssh -V` only prints its version.
hist.coeur0.1.dit: This message is written backwards! Turn it around with `rev`.
hist.coeur0.1.astuce: If `rev` gets stuck: Ctrl+C, then `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 rev message_brouille.txt`
hist.coeur0.1.bravo: `rev` put everything the right way round: the message talks about a secret passage, right here!
hist.coeur0.1.adulte: `rev` reverses each line, character by character. If a command doesn't give the prompt back, Ctrl+C stops it.
hist.coeur0.2.dit: A secret passage? It's hidden: look for the secret passages.
hist.coeur0.2.bravo: There it is: .porte_secrete! A name starting with a dot is {cache}.
hist.coeur0.2.adulte: `ls -a` also shows hidden entries (names starting with a dot), including . and .. .
hist.coeur0.3.bravo: Brrr, it's dark… There's a piece of the heart, and someone huge sleeping.
hist.coeur0.3.adulte: `cd .porte_secrete`: a hidden folder opens like any other, by writing its name with the dot.
hist.coeur1.0.dit: The heart is in three pieces, scattered across the world! Look for all the fragment objects.
hist.coeur1.0.bravo: Three pieces: one here, one in the Attic Forest, one in the Tower.
hist.coeur1.0.adulte: `find` with an absolute starting path (~/terrain_terminagotchi) and `-name "fragment*"` lists every file whose name starts with fragment.
hist.coeur1.1.dit: Glue the three pieces into one file: `cat` reads them one after the other, > pours them into coeur_repare.txt.
hist.coeur1.1.bravo: The three pieces are together again! The heart goes "boom", very softly.
hist.coeur1.1.adulte: `cat a b c` prints the files one after the other (concatenate); `>` sends it all into a new file.
hist.coeur1.2.dit: Protect the mended heart, so the Aberrations can never scramble it again.
hist.coeur1.2.bravo: Click! The heart is under lock.
hist.coeur1.2.adulte: `chmod 444` removes the write permission for everyone: the file becomes read-only.
hist.coeur2.0.dit: Abyssor, the mythical guardian, talks in his sleep. Listen to what he says.
hist.coeur2.0.bravo: He wants to know how many scratches he left in the world.
hist.coeur2.0.adulte: `cat` reads a file in a hidden folder: the relative path simply contains the dot.
hist.coeur2.1.dit: Count the files where his name is written in CAPITALS: `grep` finds, `wc -l` counts, and the pipe | passes from one to the other.
hist.coeur2.1.bravo: The pipe | plugs two commands together. Remember that number!
hist.coeur2.1.adulte: `grep -rl` lists the files (-l) that contain the word, recursively (-r); the pipe | sends that list to `wc -l`, which counts the lines.
hist.coeur2.2.dit: Write your answer (the number, instead of the ?) in coeur/reponse.txt.
hist.coeur2.2.bravo: "That is right", rumbles Abyssor. His eyes shine like stars.
hist.coeur2.2.adulte: `echo number > file` writes the answer into a file (created or overwritten).
hist.lecon.finie.dit: Lesson finished! We're doing great, you and me.
hist.libre.dit: All the places of the world are open to you! Walk to the one you want (`cd grenier`, `cd cave`, `cd tour`…) or press [a]. Type “`carte`” to see the world map.
hist.aile.suite: Another place awake ({n}/7)! Choose the next one: walk to it, or press [a].
hist.coeur.ouvert.log: 💜 The heart of the world has opened
hist.coeur.ouvert.dit: Five places awake! I can hear something beating in the middle of the world… The heart has opened: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/coeur`
hist.fin.dit: The whole Terminaworld is awake, thanks to you! But a world is big: there are still lots of letters, secret passages and quests to find. Shall we go on?
hist.fin.suite: Explore freely: quests (`tg quetes`), map (`tg carte`), monsters (`tg collection`).
hist.choisir.aide: Walk to a place (`cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/grenier`, `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/cave`…) or press [a]. Places awake: {n}/7. The heart opens at 5.
hist.aile.fermee: {chapitre}: not open yet. Finish the nest first.
hist.aile.choisie: Off we go: {chapitre}! We'll pick up where we left off.
hist.aile.autre: This is {chapitre}. To wake it up now: `tg aile {id}` (or press [a]). Otherwise, let's finish what we started first!
hist.indice.nombre: Abyssor shakes his head: that's not the right number. Count again with `grep` and `wc`, then write your answer again.
hist.indice.piece: Good command, but not in the right spot! First walk to the place {piece}: `{cmd}`
hist.menu.aide: After the nest, the order is up to you: walk to a place (`cd grenier`) or type its number. `tg aile <nom>` works too.

hist.meuble.oeuf:
🥚 A mysterious egg.
*knock knock*
Someone in there is waiting for a friend.
hist.meuble.ours:
🧸 A soft teddy bear.
Its label says: "please bring back to the nest".
hist.meuble.robe: 👗 An old dress full of dust. Atishoo!
hist.meuble.jouet: 🚂 A little broken train. Maybe we'll fix it one day, at the Workshop.
hist.meuble.recettes:
📕 The recipe book.
Apple cake: 3 apples, 1 egg, lots of love.
hist.meuble.etoiles:
📘 The book of stars.
At night, the Celestials count the stars from the Tower.
hist.meuble.abysses: Once upon a time there was a world that fell asleep: the Terminaworld.
Demons slept in its Cellar, Sylvans in the Attic Forest.
Deep down, under the heart of the world, slept Abyssor, the guardian.
He would only wake up on the day the whole world beat again.
A child and their creature would come, people said, to wake it.
They would have commands for tools, and courage for light.
The TRESOR of this world is not gold: it's the friends you find there.
hist.meuble.plan:
📐 THE CONSTRUCTS' WORK PLAN
1. Write a recipe (a script).
2. Make it work on its own.
3. Take a photo of everything with `git`.
hist.meuble.message:
The heart of the world broke into three pieces.
A secret passage is hidden right here.
Look carefully: secret passages love to hide.
hist.meuble.abyssor:
💤 Zzz… I am Abyssor, the guardian of the world… Zzz…
While I slept, I left scratches everywhere.
How many files carry my name written in capitals?
Write that number in coeur/reponse.txt, and I'll know you are worthy.
carte.legende: ◉ you are here · ▶ in progress · ✓ awake · ★ quest · 🐾 monsters · ░ not visited yet
carte.absolu: A path that starts with / leaves from the Root (absolute); otherwise it leaves from where you are (relative).
carte.lieu.decouvert: {icone} {nom}: {image}. Here we look (`ls`, `cat`), we don't touch!
carte.sauvage.lecture: 👀 System places are visited read-only: we look, we don't touch.
carte.vide: The Terminaworld is still asleep in the dark… Follow the lesson to find the old path.
carte.sauvage.dit: 🔒 We are in a system place, outside the adventure zone: we look (`ls`, `cat`), we touch nothing. The keeper looks after these places.
carte.prudence.dit: Careful: this command writes in your base camp, outside {terrain}. In the game, we build, break and move things only in the adventure zone!
carte.prudence.adulte: outside ~/terrain_terminagotchi, the game never asks you to write. System files belong to root; a normal user can only read them, and changing them would need `sudo`, which the game never uses.
carte.prudence.systeme: Stop! {lieu} is a system place: we look, we don't touch. The keeper would say no anyway ("Permission denied").

qu.acceptee.dit: New quest: {titre}! It's in your quest log (`tg quetes`).
qu.cachette.dit: A secret passage! Nobody had come here for years…

A decoration for the nest, won during a quest.

qu.suivre.aucune: There is no quest number {n} in your log.

qu.journal.bilan: Letters not read yet: {lettres} · secret passages: {secrets}/{total} · objects: {objets}
qu.journal.aide: `quetes suivre 2`: follow quest no. 2 (it shows under your creature).
qu.journal.numero: Number of the quest to follow (Enter = back):
qu.gen.perdu.texte: Someone lost {objet} somewhere in the place {piece} ({dossier_piece}/). Find the object {fichier} (`find` is your friend) and bring it back to the nest!
qu.gen.construire.texte: The monsters dream of a new hideout. Build the place {nom} in {dossier_piece}/.
qu.gen.copie.texte: Make a copy of {dossier_piece}/{fichier} and put it in nid/copies/ (build the place copies first if it doesn't exist).
qu.gen.compter.texte: A pile of pebbles appeared in {dossier_piece}/{tas}/. Count them and write the number in nid/{reponse}.
qu.gen.proteger.texte: A treasure is shining in {dossier_piece}/{fichier}. Put a padlock on it so nobody can change it.
qu.gen.mot.texte: A MOTSECRET is hidden in one of the papers in {dossier_piece}/{tas}/. Find it with `grep` and write the word in nid/{reponse}.
qu.q01.texte:
✉ Welcome letter
Welcome, little explorer! This world hides secret passages. Their names start with a dot, so you can't see them… except with `ls -a`!
There's one right here, in the vestibule. Find it and go inside (`cd`).
qu.q02.texte: 🗝 Well done, you found the secret cupboard of the old vestibule! The former inhabitants kept their umbrellas here. There are other secret passages in the world…
qu.q03.texte:
✉ Note from the mail carrier
Hello! I don't know where to drop off the mail. Can you build a mailbox in the vestibule? A place called boite_aux_lettres will do (`mkdir`).
qu.q04.texte: 🐾 Hi, it's Pantoufle, a little Monstrous Beast! My paws are cold on these old stones. Will you put down a rug for me? An object tapis.txt in the vestibule would be perfect (`touch`).
qu.q05.texte: 🕰 The vestibule clock has stopped. Ask the world for the time and write it in vestibule/heure.txt: `date > vestibule/heure.txt`
qu.q06.texte:
🛒 Shopping list
Write at least three things to eat in nid/courses.txt, one per line. Tip: `echo apple >> nid/courses.txt` adds a line at the end.
qu.q07.texte: 🐾 I'm Grignote, the vestibule mouse. Your nest looks so cosy… Will you make me a cushion? An object nid/coussin.txt will do.
qu.q08.texte: 🧸 Under the bed there are always forgotten treasures… and dust bunnies. You found a hideout!
qu.q09.texte:
📜 Grandma's recipe
Sunday cake: 2 apples, 1 smile, a pinch of patience.
Make a copy of it in your nest, just in case: `cp nid/recette_de_mamie.txt nid/recette_copie.txt`
qu.q10.texte: 📔 A diary page is waiting for you: nid/journal_intime.txt. Add a sentence about your day at the end, with >> (with a single >, you wipe everything!).
qu.q10.page:
Dear diary,
Today I found an egg.
qu.q11.texte: 🐾 Hello, I'm Mousseline the Sylvan! The vines hid my 3 socks in the Attic Forest. Bring them all back to grenier/panier/. Tip: `find grenier -name "chaussette*"` (even the hidden corners!).
qu.q12.texte: 🦉 Hoo hoo! You found the owl's secret nest, high up in the branches. It leaves you a feather as a keepsake.
qu.q13.texte:
✉ Letter from the gardener
The vines grew leaves in grenier/lianes/. How many are there? Count them (`ls`, or `ls | wc -l`) and write the number in grenier/reponse_jardinier.txt.
qu.q14.texte: 🐾 It's Ronce! My photos are lying around in the mess. Put all the photo_*.txt into grenier/album/. Tip: `mv` moves several files at once with *.
qu.q15.texte:
📢 THEFT NOTICE
A cake has disappeared! It was seen heading for a barrel in the Cellar… Find gateau.txt (`find`) and bring it back to the nest.
qu.q16.texte: 🐾 I'm Braise, a little Demon… a nice one! I'd like a chest that nobody can damage. Create cave/coffre.txt, then put a padlock on it (`chmod 444`).
qu.q17.texte: 🕳 A trapdoor under the cavern's barrels! It's cold down there and smells of cheese. A crystal shines in a corner.
qu.q18.texte:
📋 Inventory to check
How many lines are there in cave/inventaire.txt? Count them with `wc -l` and write the number in cave/reponse_inventaire.txt.
qu.q18.choses: apples, pears, carrots, cheese, jam, honey, bread, nuts, milk, eggs, soup, biscuits
qu.q19.texte:
🌲 Map of the foundations
The whole Terminaworld starts from the Root: the folder /. Look at it with `ls /`… but touch nothing: these are the keeper's places!
qu.q20.texte: 🐾 Bloop! It's Glouglou the Abyssal. I forgot the magic word of my aquarium! It's written in a diary on shelf b, after “MOT MAGIQUE”. Find it (`grep`) and write it in bibliotheque/mot_magique.txt.
qu.q20.journal:
Glouglou's logbook
Monday: I swam.
Tuesday: I swam again.
qu.q21.texte:
📚 Library card
The titles in bibliotheque/titres.txt are in a muddle. Put them in alphabetical order in bibliotheque/titres_ranges.txt: `sort bibliotheque/titres.txt > bibliotheque/titres_ranges.txt`
qu.q21.titres: The greedy dragon, A mouse on the moon, Zebedee the zebra, The pirates of the lagoon, My friend the robot, Goodnight ghosts, Alice and the golden key, Journey to the bottom of the volcano

One of the pipes (rouge, bleu or vert) in salle_des_machines/tuyaux/ is blocked by something heavy. Weigh them with `du -sh`, then write the name of the heaviest folder in salle_des_machines/reponse_tuyau.txt.

qu.q29.texte: 🐾 Oooh… I'm a friendly Undead. I can't count the awake programs, there are too many! Count them for me: `ps aux | wc -l`

qu.q31.texte: 👻 Boo! Under the mist, there was… only a forgotten shooting star. The Undead use it as a night light.
qu.q32.texte: 🌙 Ghosts only fall asleep with a story. Read them dortoir/conte_du_soir.txt page by page, with `less` (q to close).

qu.q34.texte: 🐾 Beep! I'm Boulon the Construct. Write a recipe atelier/bonjour.`sh` that says hello (`echo 'echo Hello!' > atelier/bonjour.sh`), then run it with sh.
qu.q35.texte:

The machine atelier/machine.sh won't start: it isn't allowed to! Make it executable (`chmod +x`), then try it: `./atelier/machine.sh`
qu.q36.texte: 🔩 Under the workbench, a hideout full of golden bolts! The Constructs keep their most precious bits here.
qu.q37.texte:
📷 Logbook
An album with only one photo is sad! Change a file in the carnet, then take a second photo: `git add`, then `git commit -m "second memory"`.
qu.q38.texte: 🐾 It's Nuage the Celestial! Did you know our world has an address all of its own, 127.0.0.1? Shout “Ahoy!” at it: `ping -c 1 127.0.0.1`
qu.q39.titre: The map of the keeper's places
qu.q39.texte:
🌲 Map of the keeper's places
The Terminaworld is the whole computer. Its name is written in the hall of rules, /etc/hostname: read it with `cat`. Over there, we look but we touch nothing!

qu.q41.texte:
📨 Telegram
What is the address of the world example.com? Ask the directory (`nslookup example.com`) and write the address in tour/adresse.txt.
qu.q42.texte: 🐾 Olleh! … Sorry: hello! I'm Bizarre the Aberration, I speak backwards. Write "terminagotchi" backwards in coeur/envers.txt: `echo terminagotchi | rev > coeur/envers.txt`

intro.e.texte.3: There is only one way to wake it up: type commands in the command prompt. It is the line where you write orders to the computer. It is a real terminal, just like the one computer experts use!

hist.racine.0.dit: The whole Terminaworld has a starting point: {racine}, the foot of the great tree where every path begins. Let's go! The path of the Root is written with a single slash: /.
hist.racine.0.bravo: Here we are at {racine}! The whole computer starts from here.
hist.racine.0.adulte: `cd /` goes to the root of the single directory tree: every file on the system is somewhere under /, even disks and USB sticks (mounted in /media/<name> on Ubuntu, /run/media/<name> on Fedora, /Volumes on macOS). On Windows, the root is C:\.
hist.racine.1.dit: Look around you: these are the great places of the Terminaworld.
hist.racine.1.bravo: home is {village}; etc, the hall of rules; bin, the command armoury; tmp, the wasteland… Here we look, we don't touch!
hist.racine.1.adulte: `ls` at the root shows the standard directories (FHS): /home (users), /etc (configuration), /bin and /usr (programs), /tmp (temporary files), /var (changing data, including /var/log, the logs), /dev and /proc (special files provided by the kernel).
hist.racine.2.bravo: The sign just says "/": that's {racine}, the start of every path.
hist.racine.2.adulte: `pwd` always prints an absolute path, starting with /; here it is just /. Each following / separates one level of the tree.
hist.racine.3.dit: Go back to {camp} in one go: its nickname is ~.
hist.racine.3.bravo: Back at camp! Its full path is {chemin}: the Root → the village → your base camp.
hist.racine.3.adulte: The shell replaces `~` with your home directory ($HOME, here {chemin}); `cd` on its own does the same. On Linux, home directories live in /home (on macOS, in /Users).
hist.racine.4.dit: A path that starts with / works from anywhere: it's {chemin_absolu}. Go to the hall with the full path, in a single command (Tab completes names!).
hist.racine.4.bravo: Well done, you know both kinds of paths: `cd vestibule` is {chemin_relatif}; `cd /…/vestibule` is {chemin_absolu}.
hist.racine.4.adulte: An absolute path starts with / and leaves from the root; a relative path leaves from the current directory (. here, .. the parent). `~/terrain_terminagotchi/vestibule` is absolute too once `~` is replaced. Same in a real Linux or macOS terminal.
hist.gardien.0.dit: Welcome to {systeme}! The world's keeper keeps the rules in a hall: the hall of rules. Read the world's name, written on its door. (We look, we don't touch!)
hist.gardien.0.bravo: That's the name of this world! The keeper wrote it in the hall of rules.
hist.gardien.0.adulte: /etc holds the system configuration; /etc/hostname gives the machine's name (like the `hostname` command, which also works on macOS where this file doesn't exist). Most of these files can be read freely (not /etc/shadow, the encrypted passwords); only root (the administrator) can change them.
hist.gardien.1.dit: Visit the armoury: that's where every command you type sleeps.
hist.gardien.1.bravo: All these weapons are commands! ls, cat, mkdir… each one sleeps here until you call it.
hist.gardien.1.adulte: /bin and /usr/bin hold the executables; when you type `ls`, the shell looks for an ls file in the directories of the PATH variable (`echo $PATH`, `which ls`).
hist.gardien.2.dit: Walk past the archives: the keeper writes down everything that happens in the world.
hist.gardien.2.bravo: Registers everywhere! Some are secret: only the keeper can read them.
hist.gardien.2.adulte: /var/log holds the system logs (logins, boot, errors). Many are readable only by root; on recent systems, `journalctl` shows them.
hist.gardien.3.dit: Who has the key to the hall of rules? Look at the padlocks on the door.
hist.gardien.3.bravo: The owner is root: the world's keeper. You are only allowed to read (r). If you tried to write here, the keeper would say no: "Permission denied".
hist.gardien.3.adulte: `ls -l` shows the owner (root) and the permissions rw-r--r--: root can write, everyone else can only read. Changing this file would need `sudo`, the keeper's key, which the game never uses.
lieu.racine.i: the foot of the great tree, where every path in the world begins
lieu.racine.t: /: the root of the single directory tree; every absolute path starts with /.
lieu.village.i: the houses of everyone who lives in the world
lieu.village.t: /home: the users' home directories (/Users on macOS).
lieu.camp.i: your very own house; its nickname is ~
lieu.camp.t: ~ = $HOME, your home directory (/home/<name>); the shell replaces ~ with that path.
lieu.zone.i: the playground: the only place where we build and break things
lieu.zone.t: ~/terrain_terminagotchi: the game's sandbox, the only folder where it creates, moves or deletes files.
lieu.regles.i: the world's rules, which only the keeper can change
lieu.regles.t: /etc: the system configuration (hostname, os-release, hosts, passwd), writable only by root.
lieu.armurerie.i: where all the commands sleep, ready to help
lieu.armurerie.t: /bin, /usr/bin: the executables; the PATH variable tells the shell where to look for them.
lieu.vague.i: you leave things there and they blow away by themselves
lieu.archives.i: the register where the keeper writes down everything that happens
lieu.archives.t: /var/log: the system logs (often readable only by root; see also journalctl).
lieu.portails.i: a magic place: doors to the screen, the disk… and a black hole
lieu.portails.t: /dev: the device files; /dev/null throws away everything written to it.
lieu.miroir.i: a magic place: a mirror that shows what every program is doing, live
lieu.miroir.t: /proc: a pseudo-filesystem from the kernel (/proc/cpuinfo, /proc/<pid>); nothing in it is stored on disk.
lieu.systeme.i: a corner of the world tidied by the keeper
lieu.systeme.t: a system directory, outside your home directory: read-only for a normal user.
terme.camp: your base camp (~, your home folder)

core.inconnue.casse: “{cmd}” with capital letters doesn't exist: commands are written in small letters. Type `{proche}`.
core.rate.log: tasted “{cmd}”, but it didn't work (no points)
core.err.introuvable: 🤔 “No such file or directory”: “{nom}” doesn't exist where you are ({ici}). Look at the names with `ls`, or use Tab.
core.err.refuse: 🔒 “Permission denied” = access refused: there is a padlock on “{nom}”. `ls -l` shows the permissions.
core.err.est_dossier: 📁 “Is a directory”: “{nom}” is a place (a folder), not an object. Look inside with `ls {nom}`.
core.err.pas_dossier: 📄 “Not a directory”: “{nom}” is an object (a file), not a place: you can't walk into it. Read it with `cat {nom}`.
core.err.pas_lance: 🔒 “Permission denied”: “{nom}” is not allowed to run. `chmod +x {nom}` gives it that right.

vrai.mac: 💻 In a real terminal: the same on Linux; on macOS, type `{mac}` instead.
vrai.absent: 💻 In a real terminal: `{cmd}` is not installed everywhere; an adult can add it (their password will be needed).

core.sur.lien: 🔗 Careful: {lien} is a symbolic link (it leads to {cible}, outside my zone). I never write through a link, so nothing gets damaged elsewhere. To remove it (only the link goes, not what it points to): `{cmd}`
core.sur.lien.adulte: For grown-ups: the game only writes in ~/terrain_terminagotchi and ~/.terminagotchi, and refuses any path that goes through a symbolic link (it could lead to your real files or to another git repository). {lien} is left as it is; nothing was written through it.
core.sur.lien.court: 🔗 {lien} is a symbolic link: I don't write through it.
core.sur.droits: 🔒 I can't get into {chemin} any more: its permissions were removed (with `chmod`?). To give me the key back: `{cmd}`
core.sur.plein: 💾 No more room to write in {chemin} (is the disk full?). Free up a little space: I'll try again by myself.
core.sur.systeme: ⚠ The computer refused to write in {chemin} ({erreur}). I'll try again next turn.
core.sur.bug: 😵 Oops, I tripped over a bug. Nothing is lost. For grown-ups: the details are stored in {fichier}.
core.sur.restaure: 🩹 My save was damaged: I went back to my last good copy ({copie}). The damaged file is kept next to it, in ~/.terminagotchi ({casse}).
core.sur.inaccessible: 🔒 I can't open my save in {chemin}: its permissions were removed. Nothing is lost! To give me the key back: `{cmd}`
core.sur.abimee: 🩹 My save {chemin} is damaged and I have no good backup copy. I won't erase it: run `tg` again, I'll put it aside before hatching a new egg.
core.sur.abimee.nouvelle: 🩹 The old save was damaged (with no backup copy): I kept it in {casse}, nothing is erased. A new egg is coming.
core.sur.pas_sauve: 💾 I couldn't save the game: {raison} It goes on anyway, I'll try again next turn.

prog.pwd.limite: A real signpost is planted in the ground; `pwd` only writes the path from the Root.
prog.pwd.idee: `pwd` doesn't say who you are: that's `whoami`.
prog.ls.limite: `ls` only gives the names of the objects, in alphabetical order.
prog.ls.idee: An empty place shows nothing: that is not an error.
prog.ls_a.limite: A secret passage has no lock: the dot hides the name, it protects nothing.
prog.ls_a.idee: A hidden file is neither protected nor dangerous.
prog.ls_l.limite: The r, w, x padlocks are not real locks: root, the guardian, gets through anyway.
prog.ls_l.idee: The first sign (d or -) is not a permission: it says whether it is a folder or a file.
prog.ls_r.limite: The map only shows what is under the place where you are, not the whole computer.
prog.ls_r.idee: `tree` is not installed everywhere; `ls -R` almost always works.
prog.cd.limite: You don't really walk: only the place “where you are” changes, nothing moves on the disk.
prog.cd.idee: `cd` on its own doesn't stay put: it takes you back to base camp.
prog.camp.limite: Base camp is not the whole computer: it's only your own folder.
prog.camp.idee: `~` is not a folder called ~: the shell replaces it with the path of your folder.
prog.parent.limite: Going up is not “going back”: `..` goes to the place that contains this one.
prog.parent.idee: From base camp, `cd ..` doesn't lead to the playground: it goes up to /home.
prog.racine.limite: The Root is not a disk: disks and USB sticks are stored somewhere under /.
prog.racine.idee: A path that starts with / doesn't start from where you are, but always from the Root.
prog.mkdir.limite: A new place is empty: it contains nothing until you put something in it.
prog.mkdir.idee: `mkdir` doesn't create a file: for an empty file, use `touch`.
prog.touch.limite: `touch` fills nothing: the object it creates is empty (0 bytes).
prog.touch.idee: On a file that already exists, `touch` erases nothing: it only changes its date.
prog.rmdir.limite: `rmdir` only removes empty places: if an object is left inside, it refuses.
prog.rmdir.idee: A removed place doesn't go into a recycle bin.
prog.rm.limite: The shredder has no way back: there is no recycle bin in the terminal.
prog.rm.idee: `rm` without -r doesn't delete a place: it answers “Is a directory”.
prog.rm_r.limite: `rm -r` asks nothing: all the contents go at once, with no way back.
prog.rm_r.idee: Adding -f doesn't make `rm` more careful: on the contrary, it no longer warns you of anything.
prog.cp.limite: A copy is a separate object: changing the copy doesn't change the original.
prog.cp.idee: Copying onto a name that already exists overwrites it without warning.
prog.mv.limite: `mv` doesn't copy: the object changes place or name, there aren't two left.
prog.mv.idee: Renaming and moving are the same command: `mv`.
prog.echo.limite: Without `>`, the sentence is only shown: it is stored nowhere.
prog.echo.idee: The quotes are not shown: they keep the sentence in one piece.
prog.redir.limite: The funnel only takes the normal output: error messages go past it (you need 2>).
prog.redir.idee: `>` doesn't add: it first erases what was there.
prog.ajout.limite: `>>` always sticks at the bottom, never in the middle.
prog.ajout.idee: If the file doesn't exist, `>>` creates it: that is not an error.
prog.cat.limite: `cat` shows everything at once: for a long book, `less` turns the pages.
prog.cat.idee: `cat` doesn't change the file: it only reads it.
prog.less.limite: The phone doesn't have `less`: there, `cat` shows everything at once.
prog.less.idee: `less` changes nothing; you leave it with the q key.
prog.head.limite: `head` doesn't cut the file: it only shows its beginning.
prog.head.idee: Without -n, `head` shows 10 lines, not just one.
prog.wc.limite: `wc -l` counts line breaks: a last line without a line break is not counted.
prog.wc.idee: `wc -c` counts bytes, not letters: “é” takes two.
prog.grep.limite: The magnifying glass shows whole lines, not just the word found.
prog.grep.idee: `grep` tells capital and small letters apart (except with -i).
prog.find.limite: `find` searches by name, not in what is written inside: that's `grep`.
prog.find.idee: Without quotes, the star can be replaced too early by the shell.
prog.sort.limite: `sort` sorts lines, not the words of one line.
prog.sort.idee: Without -n, 10 comes before 9: `sort` compares characters, not numbers.
prog.tuyau.limite: Nothing really flows: the system passes the text from one program to the other, which run at the same time.
prog.tuyau.idee: The pipe doesn't carry files, only the text the first command shows.
prog.rev.limite: `rev` turns each line around, not the order of the lines (that's `tac`).
prog.rev.idee: `rev` doesn't change the file: it shows the reversed text.
prog.chmod.limite: Padlocks protect against mistakes, not thieves: root and the owner can remove them.
prog.chmod.idee: `chmod 444` doesn't stop the file being deleted: that depends on the permissions of the place that contains it.
prog.whoami.limite: The game calls you explorer, but the system only knows your user name.
prog.whoami.idee: `whoami` doesn't give the computer's name: that's `hostname`.
prog.id.limite: The clubs (the groups) are not friends: they are lists of shared permissions.
prog.id.idee: UID 0 is not “nobody”: it's root, the guardian.
prog.sudo.limite: The guardian's key is not a game power: with it, one mistake can damage the whole computer.
prog.sudo.idee: `sudo` doesn't make a command more correct, only more powerful.
prog.systeme.limite: The system places are not scenery: they are the real files that make the computer work.
prog.systeme.idee: Being able to read a system file doesn't mean being able to change it.
prog.hostname.limite: The world's name is not its address: on the network, you find it by its IP address.
prog.hostname.idee: You don't change the machine's name without the guardian's key (root).
prog.ps.limite: A process is not a window: many run without showing anything.
prog.ps.idee: `ps` on its own only shows the processes of this terminal; `ps aux` shows them all.
prog.fond.limite: The faraway nap doesn't travel: the process stays on the same machine, it just no longer blocks the terminal.
prog.fond.idee: A background task is not stopped: it is still working.
prog.kill.limite: `kill` erases nothing: it sends a message (a signal) asking the process to stop.
prog.kill.idee: `kill` doesn't only stop: it can send other signals (`kill -l` lists them).
prog.free.limite: The work table (the RAM) is wiped when you switch off; the disk keeps everything.
prog.free.idee: Memory taken by the cache is not lost: the system gives it back when it needs it.
prog.du.limite: `du` weighs what is stored on the disk, in whole blocks: a tiny file often weighs 4.0K.
prog.df.limite: `df` talks about whole disks, not a single folder.
prog.df.idee: kB and KiB are not the same: `df -h` counts by 1024, `df -H` by 1000.
prog.uptime.limite: `uptime` counts since the last start-up, not since the computer was bought.
prog.uptime.idee: The “load average” is not a percentage.
prog.uname.limite: `uname` gives the name of the kernel (Linux), not of the distribution (Fedora, Ubuntu).
prog.uname.idee: Android has a Linux kernel too.
prog.getprop.limite: The phone's properties are written by the maker: they are not measurements.
prog.getprop.idee: `getprop` doesn't exist on a computer: it belongs to Android.
prog.date.limite: The clock comes from the computer: if it is wrong, `date` is wrong too.
prog.date.idee: Computers count time in seconds since 1 January 1970.
prog.script.limite: A recipe doesn't think: the shell reads the lines one by one, in order.
prog.script.idee: A script doesn't need the x permission for `sh file`, only for `./file`.
prog.alias.limite: A nickname is forgotten when you close the terminal, unless it is written in ~/.bashrc.
prog.alias.idee: An alias doesn't create a program: the shell only replaces the word with its text.
prog.fonction.limite: A function is also forgotten when you close, unless it is written in ~/.bashrc (or ~/.tgrc).
prog.fonction.idee: The empty brackets receive nothing: the words you give arrive in $1, $2…
prog.config_shell.limite: ~/.bashrc is read again when a new terminal opens; `source` reads it again straight away.
prog.config_shell.idee: Writing in ~/.bashrc doesn't change terminals that are already open.
prog.boucle.limite: The loop guesses nothing: it repeats for each word of the list, no more, no less.
prog.boucle.idee: The loop variable doesn't disappear afterwards: it keeps its last value.
prog.condition.limite: `if` doesn't understand sentences: it only checks whether a command succeeds.
prog.condition.idee: The spaces around [ and ] are required: [ is a command.
prog.git_depot.limite: The album doesn't take photos on its own: nothing is kept without `git add` and `git commit`.
prog.git_depot.idee: Git is not GitHub: Git works without the Internet, on your computer.
prog.git_photo.limite: A photo (a commit) only keeps what was added with `git add`.
prog.git_photo.idee: A commit sends nothing to the Internet: `git push` is what sends.
prog.git_histoire.limite: `git diff` compares with the last photo, not with yesterday.
prog.git_histoire.idee: `git log` doesn't show the contents of files, only the photos and their messages.
prog.ping.limite: The echo is not a sound: it's a small packet of data making the round trip.
prog.ping.idee: A ping with no answer doesn't mean the site is down: some never answer.
prog.ip.limite: An IP address looks like a house number, but it changes when you change network.
prog.ip.idee: 127.0.0.1 is not a faraway machine: it's the computer itself.
prog.curl.limite: The postman brings back the page as text (HTML): he doesn't display it like a browser.
prog.curl.idee: `curl -I` doesn't download the page: only its headers.
prog.dns.limite: A real phone book doesn't change every hour; DNS does (time to live, TTL).
prog.dns.idee: The Internet and the Web are not the same thing.
prog.ssh.limite: The encrypted tunnel hides what goes through it, not the fact that you are connecting.
prog.ssh.idee: `ssh -V` opens no connection: it only shows the version.
prog.traceroute.limite: The relays shown are the ones that answer: some stay silent (* * *).
prog.traceroute.idee: The route is not always the same from one time to the next.
prog.termux.limite: These commands talk to the phone (torch, vibrator): they don't exist on a computer.
prog.termux.idee: Termux is not all of Android: it's an app that gives a Linux terminal.
prog.am.limite: `am` asks Android to open an app: Android decides.
prog.am.idee: A package name (com.android.settings) is not the app's displayed name.
prog.appli.limite: These commands are game shortcuts: a real Android terminal uses `am` or `termux-…`.
prog.appli.idee: A game command doesn't work in another terminal.
prog.createur.limite: The level is a simple text file: each character is a square of the maze.
prog.createur.idee: Changing the file doesn't restart the game: run `doom` again to see the difference.
maths.comptage.question: Can you count objects one by one?
maths.comptage.enfant: Counting means touching each object only once while saying the next number: 1, 2, 3…
maths.comptage.grands: Counting a finite set: each element is matched with a whole number from 1 to n; n is its cardinality. In computing, numbering often starts at 0.
maths.comptage.limite: Computers often number from 0: the first box has the number 0.
maths.comptage.idee: Counting the same object twice doesn't make one more object.
maths.comptage.ex2: `seq 5` counts up to 5 in the terminal: one number per line.
maths.comptage.ex3: `ls | wc -l` counts the objects in a place: each name is on one line.
maths.comptage.erreur: Touch each star with your finger while saying the next number, only once each.
maths.comptage.kw: count counting number numbers how many digit digits one two three
maths.addition.question: Can you do an addition?
maths.addition.enfant: Adding means putting together: 3 apples and 2 apples make 5 apples.
maths.addition.grands: The sum a + b. Addition is commutative (a + b = b + a) and associative.
maths.addition.limite: In a computer, numbers have a maximum size: an addition that is too big can “overflow”.
maths.addition.erreur: Start from the bigger number, then move forward as many steps as the smaller one.
maths.addition.kw: addition add adding plus sum total together
maths.soustraction.question: Can you do a subtraction?
maths.soustraction.enfant: Subtracting means taking away: I have 8 marbles, I give 3 away, I have 5 left.
maths.soustraction.grands: The difference a − b. Unlike addition, the order matters: a − b is not b − a.
maths.soustraction.limite: Below zero, you find negative numbers: 3 − 5 = −2.
maths.soustraction.ex1: 8 − 3 = 5: eight marbles, we give three away.
maths.soustraction.erreur: Start from the first number and go back as many steps as the second.
maths.soustraction.kw: subtraction subtract minus take away remove difference
maths.multiplication.question: Can you do a multiplication?
maths.multiplication.enfant: Multiplying means adding the same number several times: 3 bags of 4 sweets make 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
maths.multiplication.grands: a × b is the repeated addition of a, b times. It is commutative and distributive over addition.
maths.multiplication.limite: Multiplying doesn't always make bigger: × 1 changes nothing, × 0 gives 0.
maths.multiplication.erreur: Add {a} as many times as needed: {b} times.
maths.multiplication.kw: multiplication multiply times product table tables
maths.division.question: Can you share sweets between friends?
maths.division.enfant: Dividing means sharing into equal parts: 17 sweets for 5 friends, each gets 3, and 2 are left.
maths.division.grands: Euclidean division: a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b; q is the quotient, r the remainder. In the shell, $((a / b)) gives q.
maths.division.limite: In the terminal, $((17 / 5)) gives 3: whole numbers throw away the pieces (no decimal point).
maths.division.idee: You can't divide by 0: the terminal answers “division by 0”.
maths.division.ex1: 12 ÷ 3 = 4: 12 sweets for 3 friends, 4 each, nothing left.
maths.division.ex3: `echo $((17 / 5))` shows 3: the terminal keeps the quotient.
maths.division.exo: {a} sweets shared between {b} friends: how many does each one get?
maths.division.erreur: Find how many times {b} goes into {a} without going over: {b} × ? must stay smaller than {a}, or equal.
maths.division.kw: division divide dividing share sharing parts part quotient equal
maths.modulo.question: Do you know the remainder of a division?
maths.modulo.enfant: The modulo is what is left after sharing: 17 sweets for 5 friends, 2 are left. It's like a clock: after the last box, you start again from 0.
maths.modulo.grands: a mod b is the remainder r of Euclidean division (0 ≤ r < b). In the shell: $((a % b)). It is used for clocks, days of the week, Caesar's cipher.
maths.modulo.limite: With negative numbers, each language has its own rule: $((-7 % 3)) gives -1 in bash.
maths.modulo.idee: The remainder is always smaller than the number of parts.
maths.modulo.ex2: 14 h + 12 h = 26 h, and 26 % 24 = 2: it will be 2 in the morning.
maths.modulo.ex3: `echo $((10 % 2))` shows 0: 10 is even (the remainder by 2 is 0).
maths.modulo.exo: {a} sweets shared between {b} friends: how many are left?
maths.modulo.erreur: Share first ({b} × quotient), then take that number away from {a}: what is left is the modulo.
maths.modulo.kw: modulo remainder left over division clock mod even odd caesar
maths.puissances.question: Do you know powers (2 × 2 × 2…)?
maths.puissances.enfant: A power means multiplying a number by itself several times: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. We write it 2³ (“2 to the power 3”).
maths.puissances.grands: aⁿ = a × a × … × a (n factors) and a⁰ = 1. In bash: $((2**10)) = 1024. Powers of 2 measure memory (1 KiB = 2¹⁰ bytes).
maths.puissances.limite: It grows very fast: 2⁶³ is already too big for the shell, which shows a negative number.
maths.puissances.ex2: 10² = 10 × 10 = 100: the small number at the top counts the zeros.
maths.puissances.exo: How much is {a} to the power {b} ({calcul})?
maths.puissances.erreur: Write the number {a}, {b} times, with × between them, then work it out step by step.
maths.puissances.kw: power powers exponent square cube itself exponential
maths.binaire.question: Do you know binary (the 0s and 1s)?
maths.binaire.enfant: In binary, there are only two digits, 0 and 1, like switches off or on. From right to left, each switch is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
maths.binaire.grands: Base-2 numbering: each position is worth a power of 2. 1011 in binary = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. In bash: $((2#1011)).
maths.binaire.limite: The switches are a picture: inside the machine, they are electric voltages, magnets or charges.
maths.binaire.idee: 10 in binary doesn't mean ten: it's two.
maths.binaire.exo: The switches {bits}: what number do they make?
maths.binaire.erreur: Under each 1, write its value (1, 2, 4, 8… starting from the right), then add them up.
maths.binaire.kw: binary base two bit bits zero one switch switches byte
