hist.biblio1.4.dit: A pipe, now! `cat` reads the whole book, and `|` sends its lines to `grep`, which keeps only the ones where Abyssor sleeps.
hist.biblio1.4.bravo: Your first pipe! The lines flowed from `cat` to `grep`. Watch them go by in the unfolded view.
hist.biblio1.4.adulte: `|` (pipe) connects one command's output to the next one's input: `cat file | grep word` is the same here as `grep word file`.
hist.port.debut: ⚓ Welcome to the Harbour! Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with its own address, and little messengers carry packets from one to another. We'll find our address, read the directory, send the postman and light our own lighthouse.
hist.port.fin: All the lighthouses are shining! You know where each machine lives, how messengers travel and how to recognise a real seal. You are Harbour Captain.
port.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Harbour
port.ouvert.dit: You can read, search and connect pipes: the Harbour opens its docks to you! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/port`.
hist.port1.titre: Who am I on the network?
hist.port0.1.dit: Look at what's on the docks: `ls`.
hist.port0.1.bravo: A sign, the harbour directory, the logbook, your dock and the teleporter. Let's visit it all!
hist.port0.1.adulte: `ls` lists the port folder the game prepared in your play area; the game writes nothing elsewhere.
hist.port0.2.bravo: The captain was waiting for you! Every biome is a machine, and every machine has an address.
hist.port0.2.adulte: The Harbour simulates a small network of 11 machines at 127.x.x.x addresses: these are loopback addresses, nothing leaves your computer.
hist.port1.0.dit: Every machine has a name. What is yours called? `hostname`.
hist.port1.0.bravo: That's your computer's name on the network. Other machines can call it that.
hist.port1.0.adulte: `hostname` prints the system's host name (/etc/hostname on Linux). A name is not an address: you need a directory to go from one to the other.
hist.port1.1.dit: And your address? The network cards are in `ip a`. Look for lo and 127.0.0.1.
hist.port1.1.bravo: lo is the loop: a card that only leads back to yourself. 127.0.0.1 is your base camp: localhost.
hist.port1.1.adulte: `ip a` (ip address) lists the interfaces with their IPv4 (inet) and IPv6 (inet6) addresses. lo is the loopback interface: 127.0.0.1/8, the whole 127.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255 block.
hist.port1.2.dit: Shout "Ahoy!" towards your own camp: `ping -c 3 localhost`.
hist.port1.2.bravo: 3 echoes sent, 3 came back: 0% loss. The time in ms is the round trip.
hist.port1.2.adulte: ping sends ICMP Echo requests and measures the reply time; -c 3 stops after 3. Towards localhost, packets never leave the machine.
hist.port2.0.dit: Your computer has its own tiny directory: `cat /etc/hosts`.
hist.port2.0.bravo: You see localhost next to 127.0.0.1: the directory says which address goes with that name.
hist.port2.0.adulte: /etc/hosts maps names to addresses; it is checked before DNS (order set in /etc/nsswitch.conf). We only read it: it belongs to the guardian (root).
hist.port2.1.dit: Ask your computer for the address of the name localhost: `getent hosts localhost`.
hist.port2.1.bravo: It looked in the directory and answered with the address. Your browser does the same before every visit.
hist.port2.1.adulte: `getent hosts` queries the system's name databases (hosts file, then DNS) the way programs do. DNS does the same at Internet scale.
hist.port2.2.dit: The harbour directory knows every machine in the Terminaworld. Look for the Fire biome: `grep feu annuaire.txt`.
hist.port2.2.bravo: feu.terminaworld lives at 127.42.0.2. Address on the left, name on the right, just like /etc/hosts.
hist.port2.2.adulte: annuaire.txt uses the /etc/hosts format. The 127.42.0.x addresses are in the loopback range: on Linux, `ping -c 1 127.42.0.2` answers, and nothing leaves the machine.
hist.port3.0.dit: The harbour lighthouse is a real little web server. Send the postman to ask for the envelope only: `curl -I http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port3.0.bravo: HTTP/1.1 200 OK: "all good". Below, the headers: who answers, what kind of letter, its size.
hist.port3.0.adulte: `curl -I` sends a HEAD request: only the status line and the response headers. The lighthouse only listens on 127.0.0.1 (loopback).
hist.port3.1.dit: Now the letter itself, but only the beginning: `curl -s http://localhost:8042/eau | head -n 3`.
hist.port3.1.bravo: The postman brought back the Water biome's page, and the pipe kept only 3 lines.
hist.port3.1.adulte: Without -I, curl does a GET and writes the response body to its output; -s hides the progress bar; head -n 3 keeps 3 lines.
hist.port3.2.dit: Put a letter in your bag: `curl -o colis.html http://localhost:8042/feu`.
hist.port3.2.bravo: colis.html arrived on the dock. You can open it with cat.
hist.port3.2.adulte: -o writes the response body to a file instead of the screen: the postman drops off the parcel.
hist.port3.3.dit: And if we ask for a page that doesn't exist? `curl -I http://localhost:8042/volcan_perdu`.
hist.port3.3.bravo: 404 Not Found: the lighthouse did answer, but that page doesn't exist. The postman still comes back!
hist.port3.3.adulte: HTTP codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (404: resource not found), 5xx server error.
hist.port4.0.dit: The ssh teleporter links two machines through a secret tunnel. What version is it? `ssh -V`.
hist.port4.0.bravo: OpenSSH is here. We won't teleport anywhere: we'll make the key.
hist.port4.0.adulte: ssh opens an encrypted session on another machine. `ssh -V` opens nothing: it only prints the version.
hist.port4.1.dit: Make your key pair, here in the harbour: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C explorateur -f cle_du_port`.
hist.port4.1.bravo: Two files: cle_du_port, the secret key you must NEVER give away, and cle_du_port.pub, the padlock you can show.
hist.port4.1.adulte: ssh-keygen creates an Ed25519 pair: the private key (mode 600) and the public key (.pub). -N "": no passphrase, only for playing here; -C: a comment with no personal data.
hist.port4.2.dit: Look at the padlock, the public key: `cat cle_du_port.pub`.
hist.port4.2.bravo: ssh-ed25519, a long string of letters, then explorateur. That's what you put on a machine so it recognises you.
hist.port4.2.adulte: The public key is copied into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target machine; the private key proves your identity without ever travelling.
hist.port5.0.dit: Write your dock's page: `echo "Bienvenue sur mon quai" > quai/index.html`.
hist.port5.0.bravo: Your page is ready. Now someone has to serve it.
hist.port5.0.adulte: index.html is the page a web server returns when a folder is requested.
hist.port5.1.dit: Light your lantern at dock 8000, just for you: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory quai &`.
hist.port5.1.bravo: Your lantern shines at dock 8000! Thanks to --bind 127.0.0.1, nobody else on the Wi-Fi can see it.
hist.port5.1.adulte: http.server serves the files of a folder. Without --bind it listens on every interface (0.0.0.0): any machine on the local network could read the folder. & runs it in the background.
hist.port5.2.bravo: "Bienvenue sur mon quai": your server answered. Your browser would do exactly the same.
hist.port5.2.adulte: curl plays the client and http.server the server: both are on your machine, linked by the loopback.
hist.port5.3.bravo: Lantern out. A server you no longer use should be stopped: one less open door.
hist.port5.3.adulte: %1 refers to job number 1 of this shell (the one started with &); kill sends it the SIGTERM signal.
hist.port6.0.dit: Watch the postman work in detail: `curl -v http://localhost:8042/`.
hist.port6.0.bravo: The "*" lines talk about the address and transport, the ">" lines are your letter, the "<" lines the reply. Several envelopes!
hist.port6.0.adulte: -v (verbose) shows the TCP connection (address and port), the HTTP request sent (>) and the headers received (<).
hist.port6.1.dit: Open the envelopes one by one: `port couches`.
hist.port6.1.bravo: The letter (application) inside the envelope (transport), inside the parcel (network), inside the truck (link).
hist.port6.1.adulte: The Internet model has 4 layers (RFC 1122); the OSI model has 7. Each layer adds its header around the data of the layer above.
hist.port6.2.dit: Write the 4 layers in order, from the letter to the truck: `echo "application transport reseau liaison" > couches.txt`.
hist.port6.2.bravo: In the right order! On arrival, you unpack the other way round: the truck first, the letter last.
hist.port6.2.adulte: Encapsulation when sending (application → link), decapsulation when receiving (link → application).
hist.port7.0.dit: Who is listening inside your computer? The open doors: `ss -tln`.
hist.port7.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is an open door waiting for visitors: an address, a colon, a door number.
hist.port7.0.adulte: `ss -tln` lists TCP sockets (-t) that are listening (-l) without translating numbers (-n). 127.0.0.1:8042 only accepts local connections; 0.0.0.0 accepts the whole network.
hist.port7.1.dit: Find the lighthouse's door with a pipe: `ss -tln | grep 8042`.
hist.port7.1.bravo: 127.0.0.1:8042: dock 127.0.0.1, door 8042. An IP address plus a port is the full address of a service.
hist.port7.1.adulte: The IP address names the machine, the port (0 to 65535) the program listening. Ports below 1024 are reserved for system services.
hist.port7.2.dit: A machine can have several addresses. Note down all the Terminaworld's: `port carte`.
hist.port7.2.bravo: 11 machines, 11 addresses, and the lighthouses linking them. Your map is written in the logbook.
hist.port7.2.adulte: All these addresses are in 127.0.0.0/8: on Linux, your machine answers on each of them. A real machine can also have several cards and several addresses (IPv4 and IPv6).
hist.port8.0.bravo: TCP opens a connection, numbers the packets and waits for an acknowledgement for each one.
hist.port8.0.adulte: `ss -t` lists established TCP connections. TCP guarantees order and delivery (lost segments are resent): it carries the Web, ssh and e-mail.
hist.port8.1.bravo: UDP sends without a connection and without acknowledgements: fast, but nothing is guaranteed.
hist.port8.1.adulte: `ss -u` lists UDP sockets. UDP is used when speed matters more than a loss: DNS, online games, live voice and video.
hist.port8.2.dit: Start the race between the TCP messenger and the UDP messenger: `port course`.
hist.port8.2.bravo: TCP delivered everything in order by resending packets 2 and 5. UDP was faster, but lost 2 packets and mixed up 2.
hist.port8.2.adulte: Same network, same losses: TCP fixes them (retransmission, reordering), UDP leaves them to the application.
hist.port9.0.dit: Your computer has a map of routes: `ip route`.
hist.port9.0.bravo: The default via… line shows the gateway: the door through which every far-travelling messenger leaves.
hist.port9.0.adulte: `ip route` shows the routing table: for each destination, the interface and gateway to use. The default route covers everything else.
hist.port9.1.dit: Follow a messenger lighthouse by lighthouse to your own camp: `tracepath -n 127.0.0.1`.
hist.port9.1.bravo: Just one hop: your camp is right here! Towards a far-away site you'd see a dozen lighthouses.
hist.port9.1.adulte: tracepath sends packets with an increasing TTL; each router that brings the TTL down to 0 replies, which reveals the path. Towards a public site, only with an adult.
hist.port9.2.dit: Send a messenger from the camp to the Fire biome: `port messager feu`.
hist.port9.2.bravo: Camp → Root → Rock → Fire: 3 hops. At each lighthouse its time to live (TTL) drops by 1.
hist.port9.2.adulte: Each router picks the next hop from its routing table and decrements the TTL; at 0 the packet is dropped (no endless loop).
hist.port9.3.dit: Oh no, a storm! Turn off the Rock lighthouse: `port eteins roche`.
hist.port9.3.bravo: The Rock is in the dark. The usual path to Fire is cut: a detour is needed.
hist.port9.3.adulte: A router failure makes a route invalid; routing protocols (OSPF, BGP…) compute another path if one exists.
hist.port9.4.dit: Guide a messenger to Fire yourself without going through the Rock. Look at the map, then give the lighthouses in order: `port guide racine … feu`.
hist.port9.4.bravo: Arrived without loss! You found the detour lighthouse by lighthouse. A packet's path can change every time.
hist.port9.4.adulte: This is source routing: the sender sets the path. On the Internet, routers choose, hop by hop.
hist.port10.0.dit: Who is the caretaker of your home? Find the default route: `ip route | grep default`.
hist.port10.0.bravo: That address is your home router (or the school's): the building caretaker.
hist.port10.0.adulte: The default gateway is usually the home router, which is also the DHCP server and NAT for the local network.
hist.port10.1.dit: The neighbours your machine knows: `ip neigh`.
hist.port10.1.bravo: Each line links an IP address on the local network to a hardware (MAC) address. The caretaker is often there.
hist.port10.1.adulte: `ip neigh` shows the ARP/NDP table: the IP ↔ MAC address mapping of direct neighbours. A MAC address never leaves the local network.
hist.port10.2.dit: Watch the caretaker welcome new devices: `port gardien`.
hist.port10.2.bravo: The caretaker gives each one a flat number (DHCP) and posts all the mail with the building's address (NAT).
hist.port10.2.adulte: DHCP hands out private addresses (192.168.x.x, RFC 1918); NAT translates them into a single public address. 203.0.113.7 is an address reserved for documentation.
hist.port11.0.dit: The lighthouse also has a sealed door, over https. Knock: `curl https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.0.bravo: curl refuses: "self-signed certificate". The seal was signed by the lighthouse itself: nobody vouches for it.
hist.port11.0.adulte: With HTTPS the server presents a certificate; curl checks it is signed by a trusted authority and carries the right name. A self-signed certificate fails (error 60).
hist.port11.1.dit: The harbour notary gave you the lighthouse's seal. Tell curl to trust it: `curl --cacert sceau_du_phare.pem https://localhost:8443`.
hist.port11.1.bravo: This time the door opens: the seal matches the one you know. The letter travelled encrypted.
hist.port11.1.adulte: --cacert replaces the known authorities with this certificate. Only trust a certificate you received through a safe channel.
hist.port11.2.dit: The notary shows you 4 seals. Read them carefully: `port sceau`.
hist.port11.2.bravo: Look at who signed, for which name, and the date.
hist.port11.2.adulte: A valid certificate: signed by a recognised authority, for the exact site name, within its validity period.
hist.port11.3.dit: Which one is the real seal? Give its number: `port sceau ?`.
hist.port11.3.bravo: Well spotted! The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that what it says is true.
hist.port11.3.adulte: TLS guarantees the server's authenticity and the confidentiality of the trip; it says nothing about the site's honesty.
port.f.localhost.enfant: localhost is your base camp: an address that always leads back home.
port.f.localhost.grands: localhost (127.0.0.1, and ::1 in IPv6) means the machine itself; the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block stays inside the machine.
port.f.localhost.limite: The base camp is not a place on the network: a message sent to localhost goes through no cable.
port.f.localhost.idee: "127.0.0.1 is my computer's address on the Internet": no, every machine has its own loopback, which never leaves it.
port.f.hosts.enfant: The harbour directory: you give a name, it gives you the dock number.
port.f.hosts.grands: Name resolution turns a name into an IP address: the /etc/hosts file first, then DNS.
port.f.hosts.limite: A real phone book doesn't change every hour; DNS answers do: they have a time to live (TTL).
port.f.hosts.idee: "The name is enough to connect": no, the computer always needs the IP address.
port.f.http.enfant: curl is the postman: it carries your request and brings back the letter with its envelope.
port.f.http.grands: HTTP: a request (method, path, headers) and a response (status code, headers, body).
port.f.http.limite: The letter isn't paper: it's bytes, and the envelope (the headers) is text too.
port.f.http.idee: "404 means the site is down": no, the server answered; it's the page that doesn't exist.
port.f.ssh_cles.enfant: A secret key you always keep, and a padlock you can show everyone.
port.f.ssh_cles.grands: Public-key cryptography: what the public key can verify, only the private key can produce.
port.f.ssh_cles.limite: The padlock can be copied as much as you like, safely; the secret key never: whoever has it can pretend to be you.
port.f.ssh_cles.idee: "The public key must stay secret": no, it's the private key you protect.
port.f.serveur.enfant: A lantern on your dock: it answers whoever comes knocking.
port.f.serveur.grands: A server is a program that listens on an address and port and answers requests; bound to 127.0.0.1 it is invisible to the network.
port.f.serveur.limite: A server isn't necessarily a big machine: it's a role, and your computer can play it.
port.f.serveur.idee: "Only I can see my server": only if it listens on 127.0.0.1; on 0.0.0.0 the whole local network sees it.
port.f.couches.enfant: A letter in an envelope, in a parcel, in a truck.
port.f.couches.grands: The layered model: application, transport, network, link (the Internet's 4 layers; 7 in the OSI model).
port.f.couches.limite: Layers aren't objects: they're headers added around the data.
port.f.couches.idee: "The Internet and the Web are the same": no, the Web (HTTP) is only one application travelling over the Internet.
port.f.ports.enfant: The dock is the IP address; the warehouse door is the port number.
port.f.ports.grands: A socket = an IP address + a port (0 to 65535); a service listens on a port, and ss shows it.
port.f.ports.limite: A machine can have several addresses (several docks), and thousands of doors.
port.f.ports.idee: "An open port is a security hole": no, it's a listening service; the danger comes from a useless or badly protected service.
port.f.tcp_udp.enfant: TCP is the registered letter with proof of delivery; UDP is the postcard.
port.f.tcp_udp.grands: TCP: connection, acknowledgements, ordering, retransmission. UDP: independent datagrams, no guarantee.
port.f.tcp_udp.limite: "Lost" doesn't mean "stolen": a lost packet was dropped, for example by an overloaded router.
port.f.tcp_udp.idee: "UDP is worse": no, it's chosen on purpose when speed matters more (games, video, DNS).
port.f.routage.enfant: The lighthouses pass the light along, one to the next, up to the right machine.
port.f.routage.grands: Routing: each router picks the next hop from its table; the TTL limits the number of hops.
port.f.routage.limite: The path can change for each packet, and the way there and back can take different paths.
port.f.routage.idee: "A message goes straight from one computer to the other": no, it hops from router to router.
port.f.box_nat.enfant: The home router is the building caretaker: it gives each device a number and sorts the mail.
port.f.box_nat.grands: The home router acts as gateway, DHCP server (private addresses) and NAT (a single public address for the whole home).
port.f.box_nat.limite: Wi-Fi isn't "the Internet": it's only the last metre between your device and the router.
port.f.box_nat.idee: "My 192.168… address is my address on the Internet": no, the Internet sees the router's public address.
port.f.tls.enfant: The envelope sealed with wax, with a seal checked by the notary.
port.f.tls.grands: HTTPS = HTTP inside TLS: the trip is encrypted and the certificate is signed by an authority, in the site's name.
port.f.tls.limite: The padlock proves WHO you're talking to, not that the site is honest.
port.f.tls.idee: "A site with a padlock is always safe": no, a deceptive site can have a real certificate too.
port.meuble.panneau:
⚓ THE MESSENGER HARBOUR
Welcome, {nom}!
Here, every biome of the Terminaworld is a machine with an address.
The base camp is you: localhost, 127.0.0.1.
The Root is the great router: messengers go through it.
Read the directory (annuaire.txt), keep your logbook (carnet_de_bord.txt)
and light your lantern on your dock (quai/).
— The harbour captain
port.meuble.carnet: # Harbour logbook: the `port …` commands write here what you discover.
port.meuble.quai: Your dock. Write here the page your lantern will serve (index.html).
port.meuble.teleporteur:
THE TELEPORTER (ssh)
To go into another machine you need a key pair:
- the secret key stays with you, always;
- the padlock (the public key) goes on the machine you visit.
On arrival, the machine sets a challenge only your secret key can solve.
No password travels.
port.page.pied: — served by the harbour lighthouse, dock {port}
port.page.404: 404: nothing at {chemin} on the harbour docks.
port.page.camp: The base camp: your own computer. What leaves here to come back here never goes outside.
port.page.racine: The Root: the great router. It knows the way to every biome.
port.page.feu: The Fire biome: volcanoes, forges and embers. Messengers arrive through the Rock.
port.page.eau: The Water biome: lagoons and currents. Its docks touch the Plant and the Ice.
port.page.glace: The Ice biome: a silent ice floe. You get there through Water or Sky.
port.page.plante: The Plant biome: forests and gardens, where Water and Poison meet.
port.page.roche: The Rock biome: mountains and caves, the usual way to Fire.
port.page.ciel: The Sky and Lightning biome: clouds and flashes, where the Celestials live.
port.page.ombre: The Shadow biome: lightless caves, linked to Machine and Poison.
port.page.machine: The Machine biome: gears and factories, between Fire and Shadow.
port.page.poison: The Poison biome: toxic marshes. A possible detour through the Plant.
port.carte.aide: One address per machine; ⇄: its neighbouring lighthouses. `port messager feu` sends a messenger.
port.retour: the messenger comes back with the answer
port.inconnue: I don't know any machine called "{nom}" in the Terminaworld.
port.messager.perdu: The messenger to {dest} got lost: no lit path.
port.messager.pas_de_route: Every path goes through a dark lighthouse. `port rallume` relights them.
port.messager.arrive: Arrived in {n} hops; it still had a TTL of {ttl}.
port.tous_allumes: All the lighthouses are lit again.
port.phare.detour: A detour still exists: up to you to find it.
port.phare.coupe: No path left to Fire. `port rallume` to relight.
port.guide.ok: Reached {dest} without loss: {n} hops, TTL left {ttl}!
port.guide.vide: Give the lighthouses in order, starting from the Root: `port guide racine … feu`.
port.guide.inconnue: "{ou}" is not a Terminaworld machine (look at `port carte`).
port.guide.pas_relie: No lighthouse links {ici} to {ou}: the messenger got lost.
port.guide.eteint: The {ou} lighthouse is dark: the messenger got lost in the night.

port.guide.aide: `port guide racine plante …`: the lighthouses in order, up to the destination.
port.course.titre: The race: 6 packets, the same network losing two
port.course.tcp: {envois} sends, resent: {renvoyes} — everything arrived, in order
port.course.udp: lost: {perdus} — fast, but incomplete and out of order
port.course.morale: TCP for what must arrive whole (pages, files), UDP for what must arrive fast (games, voice).
port.couches.titre: The letter of `curl http://localhost:8042/`, layer by layer
port.couches.aide: Write the order in couches.txt, from the letter to the truck.
port.gardien.box: The router {box} hands out the flat numbers:
port.gardien.nat: Outside, everyone sees a single address: {publique} (NAT).
port.gardien.limite: Example addresses: 192.168.1.x is private (RFC 1918), 203.0.113.7 is reserved for documentation (RFC 5737).
port.sceau.aide: The real seal: signed by the notary, for exactly phare.terminaworld, not expired. Answer with `port sceau <numéro>`.
port.sceau.ok: That's the real seal: signed by the notary, with the right name, still valid.
port.sceau.faux.auto: Fake: it signed itself, nobody vouches for it.

hist.cit0.1.dit: Look at what is behind the gate.
hist.cit0.1.bravo: The golden rule, the guard log, a chest, logs… Everything is fake and harmless: it's our training ground.
hist.cit0.1.adulte: ls lists the citadelle folder the game prepared in your playground; the game writes nothing anywhere else.
hist.cit0.2.bravo: Here we defend, we only attack the game's boxes, and never a real password. Promise?
hist.cit0.2.adulte: Defensive security only acts on what belongs to us; entering a system without permission is a crime (in France: Penal Code, art. 323-1).
hist.cit1.0.dit: Who may open the chest? Look at its locks.
hist.cit1.0.bravo: rw- r-- r--: you read and write, but your club AND the others can read. The chest is wide open!
hist.cit1.0.adulte: The 1st column of ls -l: the type, then 3 rwx groups (owner, group, others). r = read, w = write, x = execute.
hist.cit1.1.dit: Lock the chest: only you, to read and write (6 for you, 0 for your club, 0 for the others).
hist.cit1.1.bravo: rw- --- ---: the chest only obeys you now. 🔒
hist.cit1.1.adulte: In octal, r = 4, w = 2, x = 1: 6 = rw-, 0 = ---. chmod 600 = rw-------, the setting for secret files (ssh keys…).
hist.cit1.2.dit: The patrol is a script: give it the right to run, for you only (u = you, + = add, x = execute).
hist.cit1.2.bravo: rwx r-- r--: the patrol can run, and only you hold the x key.
hist.cit1.2.adulte: chmod with letters: u, g, o, a (who), + - = (how), r w x (what). u+x adds execute for the owner without touching the rest.
hist.cit2.0.dit: Who are you to the computer? Ask for your identity.
hist.cit2.0.bravo: Your number (uid), your main group (gid) and your clubs (groups). The computer knows you by these numbers.
hist.cit2.0.adulte: id shows the uid, gid and groups of the current account; the names come from /etc/passwd and /etc/group.
hist.cit2.1.dit: The Citadel has its residents and clubs. Who is in the watchers' club (veilleurs)?
hist.cit2.1.bravo: veilleurs:x:2001:gardien,sentinelle: the guardian and the sentinel. A club is a group.
hist.cit2.1.adulte: /etc/group format: name:password (x):gid:members. Here it is a Citadel example file, not your computer's one.
hist.cit2.2.dit: Hand the watchtower to the sentinel and the watchers' club. (For real you must be root: here the Citadel simulates it.)
hist.cit2.2.bravo: The tower now belongs to sentinelle, club veilleurs. Only the guardian (root) can really do that.
hist.cit2.2.adulte: chown user:group file changes the owner; it needs root rights (sudo), which is why the game simulates it and never uses sudo.
hist.cit3.0.dit: The blacksmith has a mask: it decides the locks of NEW files. Look at yours.
hist.cit3.0.bravo: Four digits (often 0022): what gets REMOVED from new files. 022 removes w from the club and the others.
hist.cit3.0.adulte: umask is taken away from the default rights: 666 for a file, 777 for a folder. 666 − 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--).
hist.cit3.1.dit: Make a secret notebook with mask 077, inside a little bubble (the parentheses) so your everyday mask does not change.
hist.cit3.1.bravo: Born already locked: rw- --- ---. No need for chmod afterwards!
hist.cit3.1.adulte: ( … ) starts a subshell: umask 077 only lasts for that command. 666 − 077 = 600.
hist.cit3.2.dit: Ask the blacksmith to explain the 077 mask sum.
hist.cit3.2.bravo: 666 minus 077 = 600: the locks are set as soon as the file is born.
hist.cit3.2.adulte: The exact sum is an AND with the inverted mask (666 & ~077), not a subtraction; it matches when there is no borrowing.
hist.cit4.0.dit: The guard writes every visit in his register. Read the last 5 lines.
hist.cit4.0.bravo: Date, time, OK or ECHEC (failure), the visitor's address, the gate, the name. The end looks calm… but let's search.
hist.cit4.0.adulte: tail -n 5 shows the last 5 lines: that's where you look first, because logs grow at the end.
hist.cit4.1.dit: How many times did someone get the password wrong? Count the ECHEC lines.
hist.cit4.1.bravo: 52 failures! That's far too many for simple mistakes.
hist.cit4.1.adulte: grep -c counts the lines containing the pattern (instead of printing them).
hist.cit4.2.dit: Who failed? Keep the address (4th word) of each ECHEC, sort, and count the identical ones.
hist.cit4.2.bravo: 50 failures for 203.0.113.66: someone is trying every password at the postern! (The rest: 2 slips.)
hist.cit4.2.adulte: cut -d ' ' -f 4 keeps the 4th field; uniq -c counts identical consecutive lines, hence the sort before; sort -n orders by number. 203.0.113.0/24 is reserved for documentation (RFC 5737).
hist.cit4.3.dit: Write the intruder's address in intrus.txt (replace ? with the address).
hist.cit4.3.bravo: Intruder spotted: the guard will close the postern. Defenders do exactly this every day.
hist.cit4.3.adulte: A brute-force attack shows up like this: many failures, one address, in a short time. Then: block it, and change the targeted password.
hist.cit5.0.dit: A glitch worm is crawling around the Citadel! Search everywhere for files ending in .glitch.
hist.cit5.0.bravo: Four glitches, one of them hidden (its name starts with a dot). find catches them all.
hist.cit5.0.adulte: find . -name '*.glitch' goes down into every subfolder; the quotes stop the shell from expanding * too early.
hist.cit5.1.dit: The worm is copying itself! What has changed since the marker set at the start of the patrol?
hist.cit5.1.bravo: Everything newer than repere.txt: the glitches, and the new one that just copied itself. 🌉 This trick will help in the Library of Time.
hist.cit5.1.adulte: find -newer f keeps files modified after f. It's the basis of digital forensics: what changed since the attack?
hist.cit5.2.dit: Delete all the glitches at once (only the .glitch files, inside the Citadel).
hist.cit5.2.bravo: Not a single glitch left! The worm is gone.
hist.cit5.2.adulte: -delete removes what find found: always run find WITHOUT -delete first to check the list.
hist.cit6.0.dit: A present arrived: cadeau.sh. Before running a program, we READ it.
hist.cit6.0.bravo: It says “Run me quickly!”… but further down there is an rm. It's a Trojan horse!
hist.cit6.0.adulte: A Trojan looks useful but hides a harmful action; the user runs it themselves. Reading a script before running it is often enough to unmask it.
hist.cit6.1.dit: Show only the dangerous line: search for rm in the present.
hist.cit6.1.bravo: rm -f bac_a_sable/tresor_*.txt: it wanted to delete the sandbox treasures. Unmasked!
hist.cit6.1.adulte: grep rm spots delete commands; a real audit also looks for curl, wget, base64, eval… anything that downloads or hides code.
hist.cit6.2.dit: Disarm it: take away its right to run, for everyone (- = remove, x = execute).
hist.cit6.2.bravo: No more x: the horse can't gallop off any more. And the sandbox treasures are safe.
hist.cit6.2.adulte: chmod -x removes execute from u, g and o; ./cadeau.sh will answer “Permission denied”. sh cadeau.sh would still run it: never run a doubtful script.
hist.cit7.0.dit: 🌉 A short detour via the Control Room: ghost processes are tiring your creature. Who is working in secret?
hist.cit7.0.bravo: miner_fictif and flood_fictif! The 2nd number on each line is their number (PID).
hist.cit7.0.adulte: They are plain “sleep” processes renamed by the game (exec -a): they only sleep and stop on their own. ps aux lists processes; grep keeps the ones we care about.
hist.cit7.1.dit: Stop them with kill and their numbers (replace ? with the PIDs, separated by a space).
hist.cit7.1.bravo: The ghosts are gone: your creature can breathe. kill printed nothing: that means it worked.
hist.cit7.1.adulte: kill sends the TERM signal (polite: “please stop”); kill -9 (KILL) forces it, as a last resort. Without root you can only stop YOUR own processes.
hist.cit7.2.dit: Look at the Citadel's guard board.
hist.cit7.2.bravo: All green: no more glitches, no more ghosts. Defenders watch boards like this all day long.
hist.cit7.2.adulte: A monitoring dashboard (SOC) gathers indicators; here three: suspicious files, suspicious processes, world-readable secrets.
hist.cit8.0.dit: Every file has a fingerprint, like a finger. Take the treasure map's.
hist.cit8.0.bravo: 64 characters: the SHA-256 fingerprint. Change a single letter of the file and it changes completely.
hist.cit8.0.adulte: A cryptographic hash function: same input, same fingerprint; in practice impossible to recover the file or forge another with the same fingerprint.
hist.cit8.1.dit: The guard wrote down the treasure's fingerprints. Check them all at once.
hist.cit8.1.bravo: couronne.txt: FAILED! A glitch touched it. The other two are OK.
hist.cit8.1.adulte: sha256sum -c reads the fingerprint file and recomputes each one; a single mismatch makes the exit code non-zero. That's how you check a download.
hist.cit8.2.dit: Write the name of the touched object in altere.txt (replace ?).
hist.cit8.2.bravo: The crown! Thanks to the fingerprints, the guard knows exactly what to repair.
hist.cit8.2.adulte: A fingerprint proves a file changed, not who changed it; for the author you need a signature (the Crypt of Codes).
hist.cit9.0.dit: 🌉 The Locker is prowling! Before it strikes, pack the scrolls into a backup chest (an archive).
hist.cit9.0.bravo: Backup done. Just in time… 😱 The Locker has just struck!
hist.cit9.0.adulte: tar c = create an archive, f = its name (z = compress with gzip). 🌉 A Control Room notion. Against ransomware, a backup made BEFORE is the best defence (3-2-1 rule).
hist.cit9.1.dit: The scrolls became unreadable .verrou files. Take them back out of the backup chest.
hist.cit9.1.bravo: The scrolls are back, just like before! No need to pay the Locker.
hist.cit9.1.adulte: tar x = extract. Real ransomware encrypts files; here the game only base64-encoded them and set mode 000, inside the playground.
hist.cit9.2.bravo: Not a single red lock left among the scrolls.
hist.cit9.2.adulte: rm -f doesn't need read permission on the file: it's the folder (w) that decides whether its contents can be removed.
hist.cit9.3.dit: Check with the fingerprints that the scrolls are exactly the ones from before.
hist.cit9.3.bravo: Everything is OK: restored and checked. The Locker lost. 🛡
hist.cit9.3.adulte: Restore, then check integrity: a backup you've never read back is not a backup.
hist.cit10.0.dit: Here is the letter for your creature. Read it: right now anyone can read it.
hist.cit10.0.bravo: In plain text: a glitch could read it as easily as you.
hist.cit10.0.adulte: “Plain text”: readable as is. Encryption transforms the text so only those with the key can read it back.
hist.cit10.1.dit: Lock it in a one-key chest. The key here is an EXAMPLE (never your real password!).
hist.cit10.1.bravo: lettre.enc starts with “Salted__” then gibberish: without the key it is unreadable.
hist.cit10.1.adulte: AES-256 in CBC mode; -pbkdf2 derives the real key from the password (slowly, with a random salt). Typing -pass pass:… in a real command leaves it in the history: elsewhere, let openssl ask for it.
hist.cit10.2.dit: A glitch tries to open the chest with a wrong key. Do the same to see.
hist.cit10.2.bravo: “bad decrypt”: refused! Without the right key it's not “hard”, it's impossible in practice.
hist.cit10.2.adulte: With a wrong key, decryption produces invalid padding: openssl stops with an error (non-zero code).
hist.cit10.3.dit: Now open the chest with the right example key.
hist.cit10.3.bravo: The letter comes back in plain text, word for word. One key locks AND opens: that's symmetric encryption.
hist.cit10.3.adulte: The remaining problem: how to give the key to a friend without it being stolen on the way? Answer in the Crypt of Codes (public key, key exchange).
hist.cit11.0.dit: Two letters “from the Harbour captain”. Compare them line by line.
hist.cit11.0.bravo: < the real one, > the fake: URGENT, a weird link, and it asks for your password…
hist.cit11.0.adulte: diff shows the changed lines (< file 1, > file 2) and returns 1 when there are differences. port-du-terminaworld.example is a reserved name (RFC 2606): it doesn't exist.
hist.cit11.1.dit: 🌉 A Harbour reflex: check through another channel. Ask the lighthouse directly for the captain's real mail.
hist.cit11.1.bravo: The lighthouse confirms it: the captain sent nothing urgent, and never asks for a password.
hist.cit11.1.adulte: curl asks the game's lighthouse on 127.0.0.1 (nothing leaves the computer). Checking through another channel (calling, going to the site yourself) defeats phishing.
hist.cit11.2.dit: The guard wrote 6 remarks about the fake letter. Read them.
hist.cit11.2.bravo: Three are real signs of a trap, three prove nothing. Which ones?
hist.cit11.2.adulte: Classic phishing signs: urgency or threat, a request for a secret, an address or link that doesn't match. Layout or time are not signs.
hist.cit11.3.dit: Give the numbers of the 3 real signs (replace the ? with the numbers).
hist.cit11.3.bravo: Well done, the fake mail carrier is unmasked: he turns back into a shadow. Never a password by letter!
hist.cit11.3.adulte: No serious service asks for a password by message. If in doubt: don't click, check through another channel, tell an adult.
hist.cit12.0.dit: Here is a list of words (creature names). How many are there?
hist.cit12.0.bravo: 128 words. Remember that number: we'll use it to measure a passphrase's strength.
hist.cit12.0.adulte: wc -l counts lines. 128 = 2⁷: each randomly drawn word adds 7 bits of uncertainty.
hist.cit12.1.dit: Draw 4 random words: that's an EXAMPLE passphrase. (Never use it for real!)
hist.cit12.1.bravo: 4 random words: easy for you to remember, very hard for a glitch to guess.
hist.cit12.1.adulte: shuf shuffles lines; -n 4 keeps 4. The randomness must be real (people choose badly). These are examples: a real passphrase is never typed into a game.
hist.cit12.2.dit: How long would a glitch take to guess? Ask the Citadel to compare.
hist.cit12.2.bravo: Short and complicated: an instant. 6 random words: centuries. Length beats weird symbols!
hist.cit12.2.adulte: Assumption: a billion guesses per second against a stolen hash. A known password falls in a split second (leak lists); 6 words out of 7776 ≈ 77 bits. Add a password manager and two-factor authentication.
hist.cit13.0.dit: Boxes are little trap-worlds made by the game. Round 1: the investigation (find 2 flags). Round 2: the rampart (repair). Look at the list.
hist.cit13.0.bravo: Three easy boxes to start. We attack ONLY the game's boxes: they belong to you.
hist.cit13.0.adulte: Like on Root-Me or Hack The Box: a “user” flag then a “root” flag (here entry and dungeon), then the fix, checked by the inspector who replays the attack.
hist.cit13.1.dit: Box “The forgotten cellar”: list EVERYTHING, even what's hidden.
hist.cit13.1.bravo: A .cave_oubliee! Its dot hid it from plain ls, not from ls -a.
hist.cit13.1.adulte: Enumerating = methodically listing everything. Hiding with a dot isn't protection (“security through obscurity”).
hist.cit13.2.dit: Search the whole box for TG{…} flags, even in the corners.
hist.cit13.2.bravo: Two flags: entry and dungeon, even inside .plus_profond!
hist.cit13.2.adulte: grep -r searches every file in subfolders, hidden ones included. The flags change each game (a hash of your seed).
hist.cit13.3.dit: Hand in the flags, one by one (replace ? with a whole flag, TG{…} included).
hist.cit13.3.bravo: Investigation round won! Now the Rampart round: fix the weakness.
hist.cit13.3.adulte: A flag is only proof you reached a place. A defender's real goal is the second round: fixing.
hist.cit13.4.dit: Rampart: the cellar is open to everyone (r-x for others). Close it to the others (o = others, - = remove, rwx = everything).
hist.cit13.4.bravo: Hidden AND locked: now the cellar is really protected.
hist.cit13.4.adulte: On a folder, r = list, x = go through. Without r or x for “o”, the others can neither see inside nor enter.
hist.cit13.5.dit: Call the inspector: he replays the attack to check your repair.
hist.cit13.5.bravo: Box mastered, both rounds! A “glitch” guardian creature may come to visit…
hist.cit13.5.adulte: The inspector reads the box's real permissions (stat): the fix is checked, not just claimed.
hist.cit14.0.dit: Box “The badly set permissions”: read every file's locks.
hist.cit14.0.bravo: journal_secret.txt readable by all, and ronde.sh with a w for others (rwxr-xrwx). Ouch!
hist.cit14.0.adulte: A script anyone can edit but the guardian runs: anyone could slip their own orders into it. It's a real, common weakness.
hist.cit14.1.dit: Automatically find everything “the others” can change.
hist.cit14.1.bravo: ronde.sh: the only file anyone can change. Defenders run this search across whole servers.
hist.cit14.1.adulte: find -perm -o+w: files with at least the “others” w bit set. Variant: -perm -o+r for world-readable files.
hist.cit14.2.bravo: Entry in the diary, dungeon in the patrol script. Anything badly locked can be read.
hist.cit14.2.adulte: In a real audit, a readable file holding a secret is already a leak, even if nobody has read it yet.
hist.cit14.3.dit: Hand in both flags (replace ? with a flag, once each).
hist.cit14.3.bravo: Investigation done. Now least privilege: everyone gets only the keys they need.
hist.cit14.3.adulte: Principle of least privilege: give the minimum necessary rights to every account and every file.
hist.cit14.4.dit: Rampart: remove all of “others'” rights on the box's files.
hist.cit14.4.bravo: Nothing left for others: they can't read the diary or touch the patrol.
hist.cit14.4.adulte: The * wildcard means every visible file in the folder; chmod handles them one by one.
hist.cit14.5.dit: Call the inspector for the permissions box.
hist.cit14.5.bravo: Second box mastered! You think like a defender.
hist.cit14.5.adulte: The inspector checks that no r bit (diary) or w bit (patrol) remains for “o”.
hist.cit15.0.dit: Box “The forgotten secrets”: list everything, hidden files included.
hist.cit15.0.bravo: A .historique_fictif and a config.ini… Secrets love places like these.
hist.cit15.0.adulte: The shell history (~/.bash_history) keeps everything typed, including a password written in a command. Here it is a fake history.
hist.cit15.1.dit: Search the whole box for the word mot_de_passe (password).
hist.cit15.1.bravo: Two plain-text secrets (game examples): one in the history, one in the config. They are the flags!
hist.cit15.1.adulte: Forgotten plain-text secrets (config files, histories, backups) are among the most frequent leaks; tools scan for them automatically before each release.
hist.cit15.2.dit: Hand in both flags (replace ? with a flag, once each).
hist.cit15.2.bravo: Investigation done. Rampart: erase what's lying around, then CHANGE the secret.
hist.cit15.2.adulte: A leaked secret is lost, even if you erase it afterwards: it must be changed (rotation).
hist.cit15.3.dit: Erase the fake history that keeps the secret.
hist.cit15.3.adulte: To avoid writing a secret into the history: let the program ask for it (without showing it), or use a secrets manager.
hist.cit15.4.dit: Change the drawbridge secret (the Citadel makes a new example).
hist.cit15.4.bravo: New secret, stored as 600. The old flag no longer works: try it and see!
hist.cit15.4.adulte: Rotation: generate a new secret, store it protected (600), invalidate the old one. The game only invents examples.
hist.cit15.5.dit: Call the inspector for the secrets box.
hist.cit15.5.bravo: Three boxes mastered! Only the great wave remains.
hist.cit15.5.adulte: The inspector checks: history erased, config.ini closed to others, secret changed.
hist.cit16.0.dit: Before the wave: which doors of your computer are open? (Read-only.)
hist.cit16.0.bravo: Each LISTEN line is a door that listens. A firewall is the list of doors we leave open, and to whom.
hist.cit16.0.adulte: ss -tln lists listening TCP ports; 127.0.0.1 = this machine only, 0.0.0.0 = the whole network. We only read: setting the real firewall (nftables) needs root.
hist.cit16.1.dit: Start the great training wave (everything is fake, everything stays in the Citadel).
hist.cit16.1.bravo: 🌊 Glitches everywhere, a ghost, a secret left open! Use everything you know, then check the board.
hist.cit16.1.adulte: The wave combines C2 (find -delete), C4 (ps/kill) and a leak (chmod 600). It's a “blue team” exercise: defending your own ground.
hist.cit16.2.dit: When you've fixed everything, check the guard board: everything must be green.
hist.cit16.2.bravo: Wave pushed back! The Citadel's towers light up one by one.
hist.cit16.2.adulte: Defending is a loop: detect (logs, board), respond (stop, erase, close), restore, then verify.
cit.f.utilisateurs.enfant: Every resident of the computer has a number and belongs to clubs: groups.
cit.f.utilisateurs.grands: An account = a uid; a group = a gid; /etc/passwd and /etc/group describe them. chown changes the owner (root only).
cit.f.utilisateurs.limite: A “club” can contain programs, not only people (www-data, systemd…).
cit.f.utilisateurs.idee: “Being admin is better for everything”: false, you work as a normal account and only ask for root rights when needed.
cit.f.umask.enfant: The mask decides the locks of newborn files.
cit.f.umask.grands: umask removes bits from the default rights (666 files, 777 folders): mode = default AND NOT mask.
cit.f.umask.limite: The mask doesn't touch existing files; it never adds a right.
cit.f.umask.idee: “umask 777 gives all rights”: false, it removes them all.
cit.f.journaux.enfant: The guard's register notes who came, when, and whether it worked.
cit.f.journaux.grands: Logs (/var/log, journalctl) are read with tail, grep, cut, sort | uniq -c: counting failures per address reveals brute force.
cit.f.journaux.limite: The game's register is invented; real logs come in a thousand formats and can be erased by an intruder.
cit.f.journaux.idee: “If the logs are empty, nothing happened”: false, nothing may have been recorded, or everything erased.
cit.f.find_newer.enfant: We set a marker, then ask: what has changed since?
cit.f.find_newer.grands: find -newer f compares modification time with f's; -name filters by pattern; -delete erases what is found.
cit.f.find_newer.limite: A date is easy to change (touch): it helps an investigation but proves nothing on its own.
cit.f.find_newer.idee: “-newer means created after”: false, it's the last modification time.
cit.f.cheval.enfant: A Trojan horse looks like a present but hides a trap: read before you run.
cit.f.cheval.grands: A script only runs if it is executable (x) or given to an interpreter; reading (cat, grep) then removing x (chmod -x) neutralises the trap.
cit.f.cheval.limite: A real trap may be hidden (encoded, downloaded later): when in doubt, don't run it at all.
cit.f.cheval.idee: “An antivirus is enough, no need to read”: false, many traps are not recognised by any antivirus.
cit.f.processus_suspects.enfant: Programs working in secret tire the computer; find them with ps and stop them with kill.
cit.f.processus_suspects.grands: ps aux lists all processes (user, PID, %CPU, command); kill PID sends SIGTERM. A process name can lie (exec -a).
cit.f.processus_suspects.limite: The game's ghosts only sleep; a real malicious process may restart itself or hide better.
cit.f.processus_suspects.idee: “kill destroys the program”: false, it stops one run; the program file stays.
cit.f.empreinte.enfant: Every file has a fingerprint: if the file changes, the fingerprint changes.
cit.f.empreinte.grands: SHA-256 gives 256 bits (64 hex digits); sha256sum -c checks a list of fingerprints. Used to verify a download or detect a change.
cit.f.empreinte.limite: Unlike a finger, the fingerprint doesn't say WHO changed the file; and if the intruder also changes the fingerprint list, it proves nothing.
cit.f.empreinte.idee: “A fingerprint is encryption: you can get the file back”: false, there's no going back.
cit.f.sauvegarde.enfant: A backup is a spare chest: you put a copy away BEFORE trouble comes.
cit.f.sauvegarde.grands: tar c (create), x (extract), t (list), z (gzip), f (file). 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offline; and test restoring.
cit.f.sauvegarde.limite: A backup in the same folder can get locked with the rest: a real spare copy lives elsewhere.
cit.f.sauvegarde.idee: “Paying the ransom gets the files back”: false, nothing guarantees it; only a backup does.
cit.f.chiffrement.enfant: Encrypting is locking a text in a chest: without the key, impossible to read.
cit.f.chiffrement.grands: openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2: symmetric AES encryption, key derived from the password by PBKDF2 with a salt; gpg --symmetric does the same.
cit.f.chiffrement.limite: The chest protects the contents, not the fact that it exists nor its size; and a weak key opens by guessing.
cit.f.chiffrement.idee: “Base64 encoding is encryption”: false, base64 decodes without a key.
cit.f.hameconnage.enfant: A fake message imitates someone you trust to steal a secret: compare, check elsewhere, give nothing.
cit.f.hameconnage.grands: Phishing: urgency, request for a secret, mismatched link or sender. diff and grep http help spot the differences.
cit.f.hameconnage.limite: A fake letter can be perfect (no typo, no weird link): it's the REQUEST for a secret that gives it away.
cit.f.hameconnage.idee: “The browser padlock proves the site is honest”: false, it only proves who you are talking to.
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.enfant: Several randomly drawn words make a secret that's easy to remember and very hard to guess. Never your real secret in a game!
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.grands: Entropy = words × log2(list size): 6 words from 7776 (Diceware) ≈ 77 bits. Length matters more than complexity (NIST SP 800-63B).
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.limite: The calculation only holds if the words are TRULY random; a known phrase (a song) falls immediately.
cit.f.phrase_de_passe.idee: “A short password with symbols is safer”: false, length wins.
cit.f.boites.enfant: A box is a little trap-world made by the game: you find the weakness, then you fix it.
cit.f.boites.grands: Inspired by Root-Me and Hack The Box, but fully simulated in your playground: enumerate (ls -la, find -perm, grep -r), then fix (chmod, erase, rotate).
cit.f.boites.limite: The game's boxes are easy and tidy; a real system is much bigger, and you never touch it without permission.
cit.f.boites.idee: “If I can find a flaw, I'm allowed to try anywhere”: false, the law forbids it outside what belongs to you.
cit.f.pare_feu.enfant: A firewall is the list of doors you leave open, and for whom.
cit.f.pare_feu.grands: ss -tln shows what is listening; the firewall (nftables, firewalld) filters who can reach it. Fewer open services = smaller attack surface.
cit.f.pare_feu.limite: A firewall doesn't protect against a trap you run yourself, nor a password given to a fake mail carrier.
cit.f.pare_feu.idee: “With a firewall I'm protected from everything”: false, it's one layer among many.

hist.crypte.debut: 🗝 A staircase opens between the roots… Welcome to the Crypt of Codes! Here we learn to hide, seal and check messages. Everything is offline, and every key is an EXAMPLE.
hist.crypte.fin: The sphinx bows: you know that encoding is not encrypting, you can seal, sign and check, and you built a blockchain by hand. You are Sphinx of the Crypt.
cr.ouvert.log: 🌍 A world opens at the Crossroads: the Crypt of Codes
cr.ouvert.dit: You can connect commands: a staircase opens under the Root, down to the Crypt of Codes! Whenever you like: `cd ~/terrain_terminagotchi/crypte`.
hist.cr0.1.dit: Look at what the crypt keeps.
hist.cr0.1.bravo: Messages, a grimoire, chests, a chain… and the sphinx's rule.
hist.cr0.1.adulte: ls lists the crypte folder the game prepared in your playground; everything happens there, offline.
hist.cr0.2.bravo: Everything is offline, the keys are examples, no real money, and the private key is never given away. Promise?
hist.cr0.2.adulte: Cryptography protects messages; here we learn it on files in the playground, never on your real secrets.
hist.cr1.0.bravo: Ym9uam91cgo= looks secret… but it's just another way of writing, like sign language.
hist.cr1.0.adulte: base64 writes 3 bytes with 4 characters out of 64; the final “o=” comes from the newline echo adds. It is not encryption: there is no key.
hist.cr1.1.dit: A “secret” message! Undo its base64 writing.
hist.cr1.1.bravo: Anyone can read it: base64 protects nothing, there is no key.
hist.cr1.1.adulte: base64 -d decodes; anyone can reverse it. Encoding (base64, hexadecimal) ≠ encrypting (you need a key).
hist.cr1.2.dit: This one is written in hexadecimal digits. Turn it back into letters.
hist.cr1.2.bravo: Readable again! Hexadecimal writes each byte with two signs from 0 to f.
hist.cr1.2.adulte: xxd -r -p reads a hexadecimal string (2 digits per byte, base 16) and gives back the bytes.
hist.cr1.3.dit: The sphinx has 5 “secret” messages. Unmask them all.
hist.cr1.3.bravo: All 5 were readable. Hiding is not encrypting!
hist.cr1.3.adulte: Common misconception: “base64 protects my passwords”. False: it is an encoding, undone without any secret.
hist.cr2.0.dit: Caesar's wheel: shift each letter by 3 (a becomes d, b becomes e…).
hist.cr2.0.bravo: erqmrxu! Julius Caesar wrote like this 2000 years ago.
hist.cr2.0.adulte: tr replaces letter by letter: a-z becomes d-z then a-c, a shift of 3 (modulo 26: after z we go back to a).
hist.cr2.1.dit: This grimoire is written with Caesar's wheel. Turn the wheel the other way to read it.
hist.cr2.1.bravo: Readable! You just needed to know the shift.
hist.cr2.1.adulte: Decrypting = the same table backwards (d-za-c to a-z). The shift IS the key; there are only 25 possible.
hist.cr2.2.dit: This one uses ROT13: a shift of 13.
hist.cr2.2.bravo: With 13, the same command encodes AND decodes (13 + 13 = 26, a full turn).
hist.cr2.2.adulte: ROT13 hides the answer to a riddle, it never protects: 13 + 13 = 26 ≡ 0 (mod 26).
hist.cr2.3.dit: The mystery grimoire has an unknown shift. Count its letters: which one comes back the most?
hist.cr2.3.bravo: The most frequent letter surely replaces “e”, the most common letter. Count from “e” to it: that's the shift!
hist.cr2.3.adulte: Frequency analysis (al-Kindi, 9th century): a substitution keeps the letter frequencies. That's why “homemade” codes break.
hist.cr2.4.dit: Give the shift to the sphinx: replace the “?” with your number.
hist.cr2.4.bravo: The grimoire opens! An ancient code breaks by counting.
hist.cr2.4.adulte: Shift = (letter found − e) mod 26. Vigenère changes the shift at every letter, but it breaks too (Kasiski, 1863).
hist.cr3.0.dit: Take the fingerprint of the letter “a”.
hist.cr3.0.bravo: 64 signs: the SHA-256 fingerprint of “a”. Always the same, on every computer in the world.
hist.cr3.0.adulte: echo -n adds no newline: we hash exactly “a”. SHA-256 gives 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal digits.
hist.cr3.1.bravo: A single letter changes… and the whole fingerprint changes!
hist.cr3.1.adulte: A good hash function shows no visible link between neighbouring inputs.
hist.cr3.2.dit: Look at the avalanche: two almost identical words.
hist.cr3.2.bravo: About half of the bits flipped: that's the avalanche effect.
hist.cr3.2.adulte: Avalanche effect: changing one input bit flips each output bit with a one-in-two chance. And you cannot go backwards.
hist.cr3.3.dit: The grimoires have seals (their fingerprints). Check whether someone touched them.
hist.cr3.3.bravo: sort_2: FAILED! Its fingerprint no longer matches: it was modified.
hist.cr3.3.adulte: sha256sum -c recomputes and compares. A fingerprint is not “decrypted”: it proves integrity. MD5 and SHA-1 are outdated (collisions found).
hist.cr4.0.dit: The guard doesn't keep passwords, only their fingerprints. Look at his (FAKE) database.
hist.cr4.0.bravo: Names and fingerprints: not a single password in clear.
hist.cr4.0.adulte: A serious site stores a fingerprint of the password; at login it hashes what you type and compares.
hist.cr4.1.dit: A glitch has a dictionary of common passwords. Read its script before running it.
hist.cr4.1.bravo: It takes the fingerprint of each known word and looks for it in the database.
hist.cr4.1.adulte: Dictionary attack: you don't “break” the fingerprint, you try likely words. Always read a script before running it.
hist.cr4.2.dit: Run the attack on the FAKE database.
hist.cr4.2.bravo: In an instant: soleil, 123456, licorne! The long passphrases did not fall.
hist.cr4.2.adulte: A short known word falls at once; 4 random words out of 128 make 128⁴ ≈ 268 million possibilities. Length beats complexity.
hist.cr4.3.dit: Real guards add salt. Look at the salted fingerprint of an example word.
hist.cr4.3.bravo: $6$, then the salt, then the fingerprint. Run it again: the salt changes, so does the fingerprint!
hist.cr4.3.adulte: Salt (random, different for everyone) defeats ready-made tables; SHA-crypt does 5000 rounds on purpose to slow down. bcrypt and Argon2 go further. Two-factor authentication helps even more.
hist.cr5.0.dit: Here is a parchment for your creature. For now, anyone can read it.
hist.cr5.0.bravo: Readable by everyone. Let's lock it up!
hist.cr5.0.adulte: A text file is in clear: anyone allowed to read it understands it.
hist.cr5.1.dit: Lock it in a one-key chest (an EXAMPLE key, never your real password).
hist.cr5.1.adulte: AES-256-CBC, symmetric encryption: one key locks and opens. -pbkdf2 derives the key from the password with a salt. Elsewhere, don't type the password in the command (it stays in the history).
hist.cr5.2.dit: Look at the start of the chest.
hist.cr5.2.bravo: “Salted__” then the salt: the rest is unreadable.
hist.cr5.2.adulte: openssl writes “Salted__”, then 8 bytes of salt, then the encrypted 16-byte blocks.
hist.cr5.3.dit: Give the chest to your creature: she has a copy of the key.
hist.cr5.3.bravo: She opens it! But how did you give her the key without a glitch stealing it on the way?
hist.cr5.3.adulte: The problem with symmetric: sharing the key. Without it, it's not “hard”, it's infeasible in practice (2²⁵⁶ keys).
hist.cr6.0.dit: Mixing paints: how two friends make a secret colour without ever sending it.
hist.cr6.0.bravo: Each keeps a secret paint, they only swap mixtures… and get the same colour!
hist.cr6.0.adulte: Diffie-Hellman key exchange (1976): g^a mod p and g^b mod p are public; (g^b)^a = (g^a)^b mod p is the shared secret.
hist.cr6.1.dit: Do the maths yourself: 5 to the power 6, then the remainder of the division by 23.
hist.cr6.1.bravo: 8! That's your public mixture. Finding the 6 back from the 8 is very hard with big numbers.
hist.cr6.1.adulte: In bash, ** is the power (the phone's shell has no **, hence 5*5*5*5*5*5) and % the remainder (modulo). The “discrete logarithm” is the hard problem that protects the exchange.
hist.cr6.2.dit: Make your EXAMPLE key pair: an open padlock (public) and its key (private). Always with --homedir .trousseau!
hist.cr6.2.bravo: Your pair is in .trousseau, the game's keyring. The private key is never given away.
hist.cr6.2.adulte: gpg creates a public key and a private key linked by maths; --homedir keeps everything in the playground, without touching your real keyring.
hist.cr6.3.dit: The creature gave you her open padlock (her public key). Lock a secret for her.
hist.cr6.3.bravo: secret.gpg: locked with HER padlock. Even you can't open it any more!
hist.cr6.3.adulte: Asymmetric encryption: anyone encrypts with the public key, only the private key decrypts. The key-sharing problem disappears.
hist.cr6.4.bravo: She opens it with HER private key, which she never showed anyone.
hist.cr6.4.adulte: That's how HTTPS works (bridge to the Harbour): the server publishes its public key in a certificate, and only it can decrypt.
hist.cr6.5.dit: Now the other way: sign a message with your private key.
hist.cr6.5.bravo: message.txt.asc: the message, with your seal underneath.
hist.cr6.5.adulte: Signing = computing the message's fingerprint then sealing it with the private key; everyone can check with the public key.
hist.cr6.6.bravo: Good signature: a good seal! (gpg also says it didn't check a separate file: that's normal here.)
hist.cr6.6.adulte: The signature proves who signed AND that nothing changed. A single changed letter gives “BAD signature”.
hist.cr7.0.dit: Draw 16 bytes of the computer's real randomness.
hist.cr7.0.bravo: Unpredictable! Run it again: never the same.
hist.cr7.0.adulte: /dev/urandom gives bytes from a cryptographic generator fed by real noise (interrupt timing, hardware).
hist.cr7.1.dit: The same thing with openssl, as for a key or a salt.
hist.cr7.1.adulte: Keys, salts and nonces must come from such a generator: predictable randomness breaks the best encryption.
hist.cr7.2.dit: A glitch has a loaded die (a bad generator). Look at its rolls.
hist.cr7.2.bravo: It follows a hidden rule: (5 × x + 3), then the remainder of the division by 8.
hist.cr7.2.adulte: Linear congruential generator: fast, but predictable. It must never be used to make a key.
hist.cr7.3.dit: Guess the next roll: replace the “?”.
hist.cr7.3.bravo: You win: randomness you can guess is not randomness.
hist.cr7.3.adulte: A real example: in 2008, a Debian bug made OpenSSL keys guessable (only 32,768 possibilities).
hist.cr8.0.dit: The sphinx asks 6 questions about tomorrow: true, false, or we don't know yet?
hist.cr8.0.bravo: Read each sentence carefully: some answers are “we don't know yet”.
hist.cr8.0.adulte: Quantum computers, post-quantum cryptography, end-to-end encryption, metadata: what we know, and what we don't.
hist.cr8.1.dit: Answer in order: v (true), f (false) or s (we don't know yet), one per “?”.
hist.cr8.1.bravo: Well done: no panic, no “everything's fine”, just what we know.
hist.cr8.1.adulte: NIST published ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in 2024 (FIPS 203 to 205); nobody can date a quantum computer able to break RSA-2048.
hist.cr9.0.dit: Here is the village's great ledger: who gave what to whom.
hist.cr9.0.bravo: A ledger: a list of facts, line after line.
hist.cr9.0.adulte: A ledger is a log that only grows. A ledger is not necessarily a blockchain.
hist.cr9.1.dit: Add a line at the end of the ledger (>> adds, > would erase everything).
hist.cr9.1.adulte: >> appends to the end of the file; > would replace it.
hist.cr9.2.dit: Meanwhile, a glitch changed an old line. Can you prove it?
hist.cr9.2.bravo: A line changed… and nothing says who, when, or what was there before. We need better!
hist.cr9.2.adulte: A modifiable file keeps no proof. For a tamper-proof ledger, you must link it with fingerprints (next) and share it.
hist.cr10.0.dit: The ledger becomes a chain of blocks. Open block 1.
hist.cr10.0.bravo: “precedent:”: each block carries the fingerprint of the block before. Those are the links!
hist.cr10.0.adulte: A block = data + the fingerprint of the previous block. Block 0 (genesis) has no previous one: only zeros.
hist.cr10.1.dit: Take the fingerprint of block 0 and compare it with the “precedent:” line of block 1.
hist.cr10.1.bravo: The same 64 signs: the link holds.
hist.cr10.1.adulte: Anyone can check the link, with a standard tool, without trusting anyone.
hist.cr10.2.dit: Check the whole chain with the sphinx's script.
hist.cr10.2.bravo: All links: OK. The chain is intact.
hist.cr10.2.adulte: verifie_chaine.sh recomputes each fingerprint with sha256sum and compares it with the one written in the next block (read it with cat!).
hist.cr10.3.dit: Play the cheater: modify old block 1.
hist.cr10.3.bravo: You wrote in an old block… let's see what the chain says.
hist.cr10.3.adulte: Changing a block's data changes its fingerprint: the one written in block 2 no longer matches.
hist.cr10.4.bravo: BROKEN at link 1 → 2, and everything after is no longer safe: the chain breaks link by link!
hist.cr10.4.adulte: To hide the cheating, you'd have to redo every following block (and, for real, convince every copy): that's what makes the chain hard to forge.
hist.cr10.5.dit: Repair it: put the real block 1 back from the sphinx's archives.
hist.cr10.5.adulte: cp overwrites the modified block with the original copy; the fingerprint is again the one written in block 2.
hist.cr10.6.dit: Ask the sphinx to draw the chain.
hist.cr10.6.bravo: All the links shine: the chain is repaired!
hist.cr10.6.adulte: A chain of fingerprints makes a change VISIBLE; it does not prevent it. Git uses the same idea (bridge to Time).
hist.cr11.0.dit: The 9 biomes each keep a copy of the ledger. Take the fingerprint of every copy.
hist.cr11.0.bravo: Look carefully: one fingerprint is not like the others!
hist.cr11.0.adulte: Distributed ledger: each node keeps its copy; comparing fingerprints is faster than comparing whole files.
hist.cr11.1.bravo: 8 the same, 1 different: the majority rules.
hist.cr11.1.adulte: cut -c1-64 keeps the fingerprint, sort | uniq -c counts. Consensus: we follow the majority's version.
hist.cr11.2.dit: Compare the fire biome's copy with the one that differs: replace the “?” with its biome.
hist.cr11.2.bravo: diff shows the line forged by the cheating biome.
hist.cr11.2.adulte: diff gives the lines that change (< the first copy, > the second).
hist.cr11.3.dit: Report the cheating biome to the sphinx: replace the “?”.
hist.cr11.3.bravo: Unmasked by the majority! But careful: if the majority cheats, it wins.
hist.cr11.3.adulte: The “51 % attack”: whoever controls the majority rewrites history. Consensus assumes an honest majority.
hist.cr12.0.dit: Adding a block sometimes takes work. Read the miner's script.
hist.cr12.0.bravo: It tries 1, 2, 3… until a fingerprint that starts with zeros. It stops by itself.
hist.cr12.0.adulte: Proof of work: find a nonce such that sha256(data + nonce) starts with d zeros. Hard to find, easy to check.
hist.cr12.1.bravo: nonce = 139: it took 139 tries. Checking takes a single computation!
hist.cr12.1.adulte: Each hexadecimal digit is 0 with a one-in-16 chance: 2 zeros ≈ 16² = 256 tries on average.
hist.cr12.2.bravo: 2615 tries: much longer. One more zero = about 16 times more work.
hist.cr12.2.adulte: time measures the duration. Difficulty grows exponentially: 16^d tries on average.
hist.cr12.3.dit: The sphinx shows the table: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 zeros.
hist.cr12.3.bravo: Time explodes! Real miners make billions of billions of tries: that costs a huge amount of energy.
hist.cr12.3.adulte: Mining does not create value by magic: it is a computing lottery that picks who adds the block. Proof of stake does it differently, without that computation.
hist.cr13.0.dit: Write an exchange in a file.
hist.cr13.0.bravo: Your exchange is written. But who proves it's you?
hist.cr13.0.adulte: In a chain, each transaction is a line signed by the giver.
hist.cr13.1.dit: Sign it with your private key (the one from the open padlock lesson).
hist.cr13.1.bravo: echange.txt.asc: your exchange and your seal.
hist.cr13.1.adulte: Only the owner of the private key can produce this signature: that's what authorises a transfer.
hist.cr13.2.dit: A glitch forged an exchange signed by the creature. Check it.
hist.cr13.2.bravo: BAD signature: the text no longer fits the seal. Rejected!
hist.cr13.2.adulte: Changing a single letter breaks the signature; nobody can redo it without the private key. Losing your private key = never being able to sign again.
hist.cr13.3.dit: Have your signed exchange written into the chain.
hist.cr13.3.bravo: The sphinx checked your seal and added a block to the chain!
hist.cr13.3.adulte: Nodes only accept a block if all its signatures are valid and if it carries the previous block's fingerprint.
hist.cr14.0.dit: The sphinx's showcase: how the inventions of the chain work. Technical explanation only.
hist.cr14.0.bravo: Currency, NFT, contract, consensus: each is made of the bricks you built.
hist.cr14.0.adulte: The game explains how it works, gives no opinion and implements no currency, no token, no purchase.
hist.cr14.1.dit: Everything written stays readable: read all the data in the chain.
hist.cr14.1.bravo: Everyone can read everything. A public chain is not anonymous!
hist.cr14.1.adulte: Addresses are fingerprints of public keys, visible to all: “blockchain = anonymous” is technically false.
hist.cr14.2.dit: The sphinx kept your logbook: a chain where each block is a step of your journey. Check it yourself.
hist.cr14.2.bravo: Your journey is chained: impossible to change a step without it showing.
hist.cr14.2.adulte: A tamper-proof logbook: the same check, with your own commands. It is not a currency, it is a proof.
hist.cr14.3.dit: Present your logbook to the sphinx for the census.
hist.cr14.3.bravo: The sphinx bows: the Crypt has no secrets left for you.
hist.cr14.3.adulte: You built everything by hand: fingerprints, chain, copies, work, signatures. The only rule of caution: the private key is never shared.
cr.meuble.regle:
🗝 THE CRYPT OF CODES
Welcome, {nom}! The frost sphinx guards the crypt.
THE SPHINX'S RULES:
• Everything happens here, offline: nothing leaves the computer.
• The passwords, keys and secrets here are EXAMPLES, never yours.
• gpg always with --homedir .trousseau: the game's keyring, not yours.
• No real money, no tokens, no buying: we understand how it works, that's all.
• The private key is never given away, not even to a friend.

cr.quiz.shor: A big enough quantum computer could break RSA.
cr.quiz.shor.pourquoi: True: Shor's algorithm (1994) factors quickly on such a computer.
cr.quiz.deja: Quantum computers already break all of today's encryption.
cr.quiz.deja.pourquoi: False: today's machines are far too small and too noisy.
cr.quiz.aes: AES-256 stays strong against quantum computers.
cr.quiz.aes.pourquoi: True: Grover's algorithm only halves the security in bits (256 → 128).
cr.quiz.meta: End-to-end encryption also hides who you write to and when.
cr.quiz.meta.pourquoi: False: the content is hidden, not the metadata (who, when, how much).
cr.quiz.normes.pourquoi: True: NIST published ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024.
cr.quiz.date: A quantum computer will break RSA-2048 before 2030.
cr.quiz.date.pourquoi: We don't know yet: nobody can date this progress.

cr.vitrine.titre: The showcase of inventions (how it works)
cr.vitrine.regle: Technical explanation only: the game gives no opinion, and has no currency, no token, no purchase.
cr.vitrine.monnaie.comment: A transaction = a signed line “this address transfers this much to that address”. An address is a fingerprint of a public key. The balance is stored nowhere: it is recomputed by rereading the whole chain.
cr.vitrine.nft.comment: A token with a unique number, written in a ledger and linked to an address. It usually contains a LINK to the object (an image), not the object itself.
cr.vitrine.contrat.comment: A program stored in the chain, run the same way by every node; its rules apply by themselves, and once written it is hard to change.
cr.vitrine.consensus.comment: Proof of work or proof of stake: two ways of deciding which block is added.
cr.vitrine.anonyme: Everything written stays readable by all: a public chain is not anonymous.
cr.vitrine.privee: The only rule of caution: the private key is never shared.
cr.recensement.ok: {n} blocks, every link holds: your journey is proven.
cr.recensement.morale: It is not a currency: it's a logbook you can check yourself.
cr.recensement.brise: The logbook is broken: a block was modified.
cr.f.encodage.enfant: Writing in base64 or hexadecimal changes the script, it doesn't lock anything: anyone can read it back.
cr.f.encodage.grands: An encoding (base64: 3 bytes → 4 characters; hexadecimal: 1 byte → 2 digits) is reversible without any secret. Encryption needs a key. Steganography hides that a message exists, without protecting it.
cr.f.encodage.limite: The sign-language image: an encoding is not a secret language, it is a public script.
cr.f.substitution.enfant: Caesar's wheel shifts each letter; but by counting the letters, you find the shift.
cr.f.substitution.grands: Monoalphabetic substitution (Caesar, ROT13): only 25 keys, and letter frequencies are kept. Vigenère (several shifts) falls too (Kasiski, Friedman).
cr.f.substitution.limite: The wheel shows a simple shift; real substitutions can shuffle the whole alphabet, and still fall to frequencies.
cr.f.substitution.idee: “A homemade code is safe”: almost always false.
cr.f.hachage.enfant: A file's fingerprint: always the same for the same file, completely different if a single letter changes.
cr.f.hachage.grands: Cryptographic hash function (SHA-256, FIPS 180-4): deterministic, avalanche effect, one-way, collisions infeasible in practice. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collisions.
cr.f.hachage.limite: Like a fingerprint, it identifies; but it doesn't contain the file and is not “decrypted”.
cr.f.hachage.idee: “You can decrypt a fingerprint”: false, you can only guess the input and compare.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.enfant: The guard only keeps your password's fingerprint. Short known words fall fast; a long phrase of random words holds.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.grands: Hashed AND salted storage with a slow function (SHA-crypt, bcrypt, Argon2); a dictionary attack tries likely words. Length > complexity (NIST SP 800-63B), password manager, two-factor authentication.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.limite: The game's database is FAKE and unsalted on purpose, to see the attack; a real site must salt.
cr.f.mots_de_passe.idee: “A short complicated password is safer than a long phrase”: false.
cr.f.symetrique.enfant: A chest and a key: the same key locks and opens. Your friend needs a copy.
cr.f.symetrique.grands: Symmetric encryption (AES, FIPS 197); the key is derived from the password (PBKDF2, RFC 8018). Problem: sharing the key without it being intercepted.
cr.f.symetrique.limite: Without the key, it's not “hard”, it's infeasible in practice: 2²⁵⁶ possible keys.
cr.f.symetrique.idee: “With a powerful enough computer, you open any AES chest”: false.
cr.f.asymetrique.enfant: Open padlocks handed out to everyone: anyone can lock the box, only you have the key.
cr.f.asymetrique.grands: Public / private key pair (RSA, elliptic curves); Diffie-Hellman key exchange (mixing paints); digital signature; certificates bind a key to a name (HTTPS).
cr.f.asymetrique.limite: Mixing paints is an image: for real, they are modular powers of very big numbers.
cr.f.asymetrique.idee: “You can give your private key to a trusted friend”: no, never.
cr.f.hasard.enfant: Keys must be drawn from real randomness: a loaded die can be guessed.
cr.f.hasard.grands: Cryptographic generator (/dev/urandom, getrandom) versus predictable generator (linear congruential). Keys, salts and nonces require the first.
cr.f.hasard.limite: The game's 8-sided die is too simple on purpose, so that you can guess it.
cr.f.hasard.idee: “The current time is random enough”: false, it can be guessed.
cr.f.post_quantique.enfant: Quantum computers might one day break some padlocks; tomorrow's padlocks are already being prepared.
cr.f.post_quantique.grands: Shor threatens RSA and elliptic curves; Grover only reduces AES security. NIST: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), 2024. End-to-end protects the content, not the metadata.
cr.f.post_quantique.limite: Nobody knows when such a computer will exist: the game answers “we don't know yet”.
cr.f.registre.enfant: A ledger is a big book where you write who gave what to whom.
cr.f.registre.grands: A ledger (append-only log); on its own, a modifiable file keeps no proof of changes.
cr.f.registre.limite: A ledger is not necessarily a blockchain: a classic database is one too.
cr.f.registre.idee: “A ledger file is enough to prove it hasn't changed”: false.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.enfant: Each link carries the fingerprint of the link before: touch an old link and the chain breaks.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.grands: Block = data + fingerprint of the previous block; modifying a block invalidates all the following ones. Same principle as git commits.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.limite: The chain makes a change visible; it doesn't prevent it on its own.
cr.f.chaine_blocs.idee: “A blockchain can never contain an error”: false, it keeps errors too.
cr.f.consensus.enfant: The 9 biomes each keep a copy: the different copy is unmasked by the majority.
cr.f.consensus.grands: Distributed ledger, consensus: nodes follow the majority's version (according to the network's rule). 51 % attack.
cr.f.consensus.limite: A majority can also be wrong or cheat.
cr.f.preuve_travail.enfant: To add a block, you must find a magic number by trying a lot: hard to find, easy to check.
cr.f.preuve_travail.grands: Proof of work: find a nonce whose fingerprint is under a target; exponential difficulty (16^d); energy cost; proof of stake picks who adds the block differently.
cr.f.preuve_travail.limite: The game's mining is tiny (at most 3 zeros) and stops by itself.
cr.f.signature.enfant: Each exchange carries the seal of the giver; a fake line has no valid seal.
cr.f.signature.grands: Transactions signed with the private key, checked with the public key; a signature can't be copied onto another text.
cr.f.signature.limite: The game signs with gpg (OpenPGP); chains use other formats, same principle.
cr.f.signature.idee: “Losing your private key doesn't matter”: false, you can't sign anything any more.
cr.f.applications.enfant: The showcase links each invention (currency, NFT, contract) to the bricks you built: no opinion, just how it works.
cr.f.applications.grands: Cryptocurrency, NFT, smart contract, consensus: technical operation only; everything written stays readable (public addresses).
cr.f.applications.limite: The game implements no currency, no token, no NFT, no purchase; it explains.
cr.f.applications.idee: “Blockchain is anonymous”: technically false, addresses are public.
